articles.title: Criança ganha surpresa de policiais no aniversário após mobilização | G1
articles.standfirst: Joaquim, de Presidente Prudente (SP), escolheu o tema da festa e passou a esperar pela chegada dos policiais. Para encontrá-lo, batalhão chegou a publicar um "procura-se" nas redes sociais.
articles.summary: Joaquim, de 3 anos, recebeu policiais militares em sua festa de aniversário no domingo (20). A comemoração ocorreu em Presidente Prudente (SP) após mobilização na internet.
articles.body:
Joaquim completou 3 anos no último sábado (19) com um desejo bem definido: queria policiais militares na festa para cantar parabéns com ele . Fã da Polícia Militar, o menino escolheu o próprio tema da comemoração e passou meses falando que seriam os policiais que o ajudariam a apagar a vela.

No domingo (20), o sonho virou realidade, depois de uma pequena saga para que a equipe encontrasse o aniversariante, em Presidente Prudente (SP).

A comemoração acontecia em uma chácara onde mora a tia-avó de Joaquim. A família havia deixado o convite em uma base da Polícia Militar, com data, horário e endereço. O problema é que, segundo a mãe do menino, faltou deixar um contato.

Na manhã da festa, policiais passaram pela região tentando localizar o endereço. Enquanto isso, Joaquim, vestido de policial, aguardava no portão.

A família chegou a receber a notícia de que a viatura havia atolado e precisado de um guincho. Para o pequeno aniversariante, foi um "banho de água fria".

"Para nós foi um banho de água fria. Joaquim estava vestido de polícia e toda hora olhava no portão para ver se estavam chegando. Quando viu a movimentação da gente dizendo que talvez eles não iam conseguir vir, ele ficou um pouco chateado", disse Thais Mendonça, mãe do menino.

Menino de 3 anos recebe surpresa de policiais em festa de aniversário após mobilização na internet em Presidente Prudente (SP) — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal/Thais Mendonça

A equipe, porém, não desistiu. Após essa situação, o 18° Batalhão de Polícia Militar do Interior (BPM/I) publicou nas redes sociais que procurava por Joaquim, e que se alguém da família estivesse vendo a publicação, entrasse em contato com a Polícia Militar.

Nesse meio tempo, a família conseguiu falar com a PM e enviou a localização correta, o que permitiu a chegada dos policiais à festa. A recepção não poderia ter sido mais especial.

“Quando a viatura chegou foi muito emocionante, acredito que até quem não é de chorar, chorou, eu me emociono só de escrever isso aqui. Foi surreal”, relatou a mãe.

Com a sirene ligada, a viatura entrou no local da festa. Quando os policiais desceram, o menino correu para eles.

“Quando entraram com a viatura, sirene ligada, Joaquim encheu os olhos de lágrimas [...] Quando os policiais desceram, ele se jogou para o colo deles, muito emocionado”, relembrou a mãe.

A admiração pela profissão também aparece nas brincadeiras do dia a dia. De acordo com a mãe, a ideia surgiu a partir das próprias brincadeiras do menino, já que ele sempre coloca adereços semelhantes aos da polícia e diz que vai prender os bandidos.

A família costuma assistir a programas policiais e acredita que isso pode ter contribuído para a paixão do menino pela profissão.

A mãe ainda contou que decidiu levar a brincadeira a sério e procurou a Polícia Militar meses antes do aniversário para saber se seria possível contar com a presença dos policiais.

"Eu sou uma mãe que ama comemorar. E entrei na onda das brincadeiras dele. Ele sempre falava que o policial ia cantar parabéns para ele. Desde o início já sabíamos que seria apenas um bolinho, mas eu gosto de marcar, então pensei: 'Porque não entrar na onda dele?'. Fui buscar possibilidades”, disse.

Depois de receber o sinal positivo da corporação, a expectativa aumentou. Até o momento da chegada, porém, a família não tinha certeza se tudo daria certo.

“A expectativa estava a mil, confesso que até fiquei apreensiva, porque eu tinha um pouco de medo de não dar certo, por forças maiores, e ele ficar esperando... Porque falava muito”.

A procura pelo aniversariante ganhou repercussão nas redes sociais do 18º Batalhão de Polícia Militar do Interior (BPM/I).

Como a equipe não havia conseguido localizar inicialmente a família, o batalhão publicou um pedido para encontrar Joaquim e seus responsáveis. A mobilização funcionou, e os policiais conseguiram chegar à comemoração.

18º Batalhão de Polícia Militar do Interior (BPM/I) fez uma publicação nas redes sociais procurando o endereço correto do Joaquim — Foto: Redes Sociais/Reprodução

Para a mãe, Thais G. Mendonça Berti, de 31 anos, foi justamente naquele momento que ela percebeu a dimensão que o convite do filho havia tomado: "Eu falei 'Meu Deus, olha a proporção desse convite'”.

A experiência deixou uma lembrança que, segundo a mãe, deve acompanhar Joaquim por muito tempo.

“Eu acredito que esse momento vai marcar a vida dele para sempre. Ele se sentiu especial, se sentiu querido, e disse que os policiais são os amigos dele.”

Para Thais e o pai do menino, a presença dos policiais também ganhou um significado especial.

“Para nós como pais, até agora estamos impactados com tudo que vivemos. Realizar desejo de filho é incrível, e nos sentimos honrados por ele estar crescendo e voltando-se para o lado do bem”, contou emocionada.

Depois da festa, a empolgação continuou. E o próximo pedido já apareceu: “[Joaquim] Disse que quer que eu leve ele no batalhão para ir atrás de bandido com os policiais”.

Para a família, o aniversário que começou como uma simples tentativa de realizar uma vontade de Joaquim acabou se transformando em uma lembrança compartilhada também pelos policiais que participaram da comemoração.

“Eu jamais poderia imaginar a proporção de um simples convite. Queríamos fazer o dia do nosso pequeno feliz, e no fim movemos e comovemos uma pequena multidão. Acredito que todos nós vamos guardar esse dia para sempre”, concluiu a mãe.

articles.title: Senado e STF: o poder dos senadores sobre as vagas no Supremo | G1
articles.standfirst: Senadores têm poder para aprovar indicações ao Supremo, conduzir o ritmo das sabatinas e abrir processos de impeachment contra ministros; nova composição da Casa pode alterar a dinâmica entre os Poderes
articles.summary: O Senado e STF mantêm uma relação de poder onde senadores decidem a indicação de ministros do Supremo e podem até abrir processos de impeachment.
articles.body:
O Senado Federal costuma aparecer no noticiário como coadjuvante das grandes disputas de Brasília. Mas, quando o assunto é a relação entre o Congresso e o Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), a Casa está longe de ocupar um papel secundário. É no Senado que passam algumas das principais ferramentas de controle sobre o Judiciário e é justamente por isso que a eleição para a Casa ganha peso na relação com o STF.

A escolha dos ministros do Supremo é um exemplo. O presidente da República indica o nome, mas não tem a palavra final. O indicado precisa ser sabatinado pela Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ) e, depois, aprovado pelo plenário do Senado.

Na prática, os senadores podem decidir não apenas se uma indicação será aprovada ou rejeitada, mas também quando ela avançará.

O caso de André Mendonça , indicado por Jair Bolsonaro para o Supremo, mostrou o peso desse calendário. O nome permaneceu por cinco meses à espera da sabatina no Senado. O episódio evidenciou que o poder da Casa não está restrito ao voto final: o tempo também é um instrumento político.

Mais recentemente, a indicação de Jorge Messias , feita pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva para uma vaga no Supremo, mostrou o outro lado dessa prerrogativa. Depois da sabatina, o nome chegou ao plenário e foi rejeitado pelos senadores.

Os dois episódios ajudam a dimensionar a relação entre os Poderes.

E a influência da Casa sobre o Supremo não termina na escolha de ministros. Os senadores também têm competência para processar e julgar ministros do tribunal por crime de responsabilidade, em processos de impeachment. Trata-se de uma atribuição que raramente chega a ser utilizada, mas que coloca nas mãos do Senado um instrumento de controle sobre a mais alta Corte do país.

O poder dos senadores se estende ainda a outras áreas. Cabe ao Senado aprovar indicações de embaixadores e sabatinar e aprovar dirigentes do Banco Central, além de exercer competências próprias no processo legislativo.

É por isso que uma eleição para o Senado não diz respeito apenas à composição do Congresso. Ela também pode alterar a relação entre os Poderes.

A eleição para o Senado coloca em disputa justamente essa outra ponta do equilíbrio institucional. O resultado das urnas não escolherá apenas quem ocupará as cadeiras da Casa. Também definirá quem terá nas mãos algumas das principais ferramentas de interação com o Supremo.

articles.title: Debate: candidatos ao Senado no CE discutem data centers e segurança | G1
articles.standfirst: Participaram do debate desta segunda (21) Cid Gomes (PSB) e Luizianne Lins (Rede). Alcides Fernandes (PL) e Capitão Wagner (União) também foram convidados para o debate, mas não compareceram.
articles.summary: Cid Gomes (PSB) e Luizianne Lins (Rede) participaram do debate. Alcides Fernandes (PL) e Capitão Wagner (União) também foram convidados, mas não compareceram.
articles.body:
O debate promovido pelo g1 nesta segunda-feira (21) entre candidatos ao Senador pelo Ceará foi marcado por concordância com a instalação de data centers no estado e discussões sobre a melhor forma de empregar as emendas parlamentares e de medidas para fomentar o trabalho e o emprego .

Os candidatos também discutiram medidas para o combate às facções criminosas e à violência contra a mulher, além de discutirem a relação entre os Poderes (veja, mais abaixo, vídeos de cada tema) .

Participaram do encontro os candidatos Cid Gomes (PSB) e Luizianne Lins (Rede). Alcides Fernandes (PL) e Capitão Wagner (União) também foram convidados para o debate, mas não compareceram. O debate foi transmitido ao vivo, de Fortaleza , pelo site e pelos perfis do g1 no YouTube, Tiktok e Instagram.

Foram convidados os candidatos de partidos e federações com representação mínima de cinco parlamentares no Congresso, ou que alcançaram ao menos 5% de intenções de voto na última pesquisa Quaest.

Seis temas foram previamente definidos e comunicados às campanhas antes do debate. A ordem dos assuntos foi sorteada antes do início do encontro, bem como a posição das cadeiras durante o encontro e a ordem das considerações finais.

Os participantes tiveram 15 minutos de tempo de fala para administrar ao longo da discussão, com intervenções de até 1 minuto e 30 segundos por vez. Ao final, todos tiveram direito a um minuto para as considerações finais.

Confira o que falaram os candidatos sobre os temas estabelecidos:

Cid Gomes (PSB) e Luizianne Lins (Rede) já estão posicionados para o debate do g1, às 14h. — Foto: Ismael Soares.

Primeiro tema: data centers e recursos naturais

No primeiro tema, os candidatos do Senado pelo Ceará discutiram sobre as oportunidades de empregos que podem surgir com a chegada de equipamentos tecnológicos como o Data Center do TikTok instalado no Ceará.

Cid Gomes destacou as oportunidades que os equipamentos podem criar do estado. O candidato lembrou que, historicamente, no estado, as estruturas são construídas antes de começar as atividades empresariais. Citou o Porto do Pecem, a rede de fibra ótica, a primeira Zona de Processamento de Exportação (ZPE) do Brasil e como os equipamentos tornaram o estado forte na concorrência internacional dos países que pleiteavam o Data Center do TikTok. Cid citou ainda as centenas de pessoas que já trabalham na construção do Data Center. Por fim, o candidato do PSB destacou o uso e a produção de energias renováveis para esses equipamentos.

Luizianne falou que é favorável ao estado receber grandes equipamentos de infraestrutura digital. Ela lembrou da legislação que aprovou, durante sua gestão na prefeitura de Fortaleza, as atividades de parques tecnológicos na cidade. A candidata da Rede destacou ainda a participação dela sobre as discussões da soberania digital e tecnológica no Brasil no Congresso, durante os mandatos como deputada federal.

No segundo tema, os candidatos discutiram emendas parlamentares, sua distribuição a municípios e a atribuição dos parlamentares na construção do Orçamento da União.

Luizianne Lins destacou que as emendas são provenientes de dinheiro público e que, portanto, devem chegar diretamente à população. A candidata defendeu que metade de todas as emendas parlamentares deveriam ir para a área de saúde pública. A candidata pela Rede também afirmou que as emendas deveriam priorizar regiões que têm mais dificuldade de acesso a investimentos e afirmou que, como deputada federal, prioriza emendas para o interior, em áreas como saúde, educação e agricultura familiar.

Cid Gomes disse ser favorável à participação de parlamentares na indicação de recursos no Orçamento da União, mas disse que esse processo deve ser feito com parcimônia. Cid defendeu que o Poder Executivo tenha preferência na indicação de recursos do Orçamento, uma vez que é o responsável pela arrecadação. O candidato à reeleição pelo PSB também defendeu o envio de emendas a pequenas cidades e maior fiscalização na aplicação do dinheiro.

No terceiro tema, os candidatos discutiram sobre trabalho e emprego. Cid e Luizianne defenderam iniciativas dos governos Lula (PT) e Elmano de Freitas (PT), além de propor novas medidas para a área.

Cid destacou que educação e trabalho são duas áreas prioritárias para quem está no Poder Público. O candidato disse ainda que é preciso garantir as condições de infraestrutura para que o país tenha capacidade de competir de igual para igual com os demais países dentro do mercado global. Cid afirmou que o Ceará se prepara para isso e citou obras do governo do presidente Lula no estado, como a ferrovia Transnordestina. Ele também citou que o Ceará se destaca pela capacidade de produção de energia, dispondo de três vezes mais do que consome internamente.

Luizianne relembrou iniciativas da sua gestão quando prefeita de Fortaleza e disse que a capital gerou 180 mil empregos entre os anos de 2005 e 2010. Ela mencionou ações como o acesso ao crédito, aumento de obras públicas e investimento maior em turismo, mencionando a criação de uma secretaria específica e a implantação da festa do Reveillon de Fortaleza.

Cid também defendeu ações dos governos Lula e Elmano, destacando a implantação do Polo Automotivo do Ceará, em Horizonte. Luizianne afirmou que pretende atuar nesse tema caso seja eleito senadora e citou a criação de um projeto chamado "Crédito Lilás", para financiar o acesso a crédito para mulheres.

Quarto tema: combate às facções criminosas

No quarto tema, os candidatos debateram as estratégias para combater o crime organizado e impedir que a juventude seja cooptada por facções criminosas. Ambos defenderam uma perspectiva nacional de combate aos grupos criminosos, com sistemas integrados entre municípios, estados e União.

Luizianne destacou que o combate ao crime organizado é uma questão central para qualquer governo. Ela disse que é necessário focar nas pessoas cooptadas pela facção criminosa. A candidata defendeu que é preciso focar em políticas públicas para promoção de cultura e oportunidades de emprego como prevenção contra o crime organizado. Luizianne defendeu a criação de um sistema único de segurança pública a partir de uma PEC.

Cid disse que o tema é delicado e precisa ser prioridade pelos governantes. Educação, emprego e renda permitem a juventude sonhar com outras opções, segundo o candidato. Disse que a concentração de renda permite que criminosos se aproveitem de necessidades para criar exércitos. Destacou que as facções atuam de maneira nacional e se espalham pelos estados. Defendeu que o combate precisa ser visto de maneira nacional, com contratação de 10 mil profissionais para a inteligência policial e ampliação do efetivo da Polícia Federal, que atualmente possui 12 mil funcionários.

Durante as falas desse tema, Cid e Luizianne criticaram as ausências de Alcides Fernandes e Capitão Wagner, que possuem a segurança pública como uma das principais pautas de campanha, segundo eles. Luizianne disse que os adversários reduzem a disputa pelo governo do estado à segurança pública. A candidata da Rede criticou a ausência dos concorrentes, que não puderam apresentar as ideias que têm sobre o tema. Cid também criticou os candidatos que não compareceram aos debates e disse que os candidados agem com demagogia ao abordar o tema da segurança pública.

No quinto tema, os candidatos discutiram a relação entre os Poderes Executivo, Legislativo e Judiciário, no âmbito da Presidência da República, do Congresso Nacional e do Supremo Tribunal Federal.

Cid Gomes defendeu que o STF seja fiscalizado pelo Conselho Nacional de Justiça (CNJ). Ele disse que o país vive um momento muito delicado com um poder interferindo no outro, com o Legislativo aumentando seu poder sobre o Orçamento e o Executivo legislando por meio de medidas provisórias. Cid, porém, destacou que a principal crise atualmente é a do Poder Judiciário, que viu sua credibilidade e confiança perante a população serem abalados diante dos escândalos recentes. Cid afirmou que parte do problema ocorre porque não existe um órgão responsável por fiscalizar o STF, e que essa atribuição deveria ser do CNJ.

Luizianne Lins afirmou que a relação entre Poderes define o andamento das políticas públicas e apontou que eles devem funcionar de forma harmônica pelo bem da população. Ela afirmou que todos os Poderes públicos precisam passar por controle social e destacou que, neste caso, o papel do senador também é fiscalizar esses Poderes públicos de forma responsável. A candidata disse ser contra o uso desse poder fiscalizador do Senado para promover processos de impeachment por motivações exclusivamente políticas.

No sexto e último bloco temático, os candidatos discutiram o tema da violência contra a mulher. Ambos concordaram que é preciso o apoio do Estado nesse assunto.

Luizianne Lins afirmou que esse é um "tema caro" para ela e que possui trajetória e compromisso de luta de combate à violência contra mulheres. Ela citou novamente ações da sua gestão à frente da Prefeitura de Fortaleza e destacou que, naquela época, já foram criadas políticas específicas nessa área, citando o Centro de Referência Francisca Clotilde e um programa municipal de prevenção e tratamento, proporcionando uma "rede integrada de atendimento".

A candidata ainda destacou que é a presidente da Comissão Permanente Mista de Combate à Violência contra a Mulher no Congresso Nacional e que, nesse espaço, são discutidos mecanismos concretos para prevenir e evitar casos de feminicídios. Luizianne também mencionou que, durante o seu mandato na Câmara dos Deputados, aprovou a chamada Lei Lola, que fez com que a Polícia Federal (PF) pudesse investigar crimes contra mulheres no ambiente digital.

Já Cid Gomes afirmou que o machismo vem desde casa e defendeu que o sistema educacional discuta a questão e promova a noção do respeito às mulheres desde a primeira infância.

Cid falou sobre educação. Destacou que o tema precisa ser um dos principais focos do governo, especialmente voltado para o público em vulnerabilidade social. Cid defendeu que as séries finais do ensino fundamental sejam realizadas em tempo integral. O candidato do PSB destacou ainda o foco em alfabetização na idade certa e vagas em universidades públicas para a população mais pobre. Cid falou ainda sobre saúde pública. O candidato defendeu ampliação da atenção primária na rede municipal, centros de especialidades médicas em microrregiões e hospitais regionais nas macrorregiões-polos do estado.

Luizianne destacou políticas públicas para as mulheres. A candidata da Rede disse que é preciso protagonismo das mulheres em todas as áreas. Ela criticou a chapa adversária (onde estão os candidatos Alcides Fernandes e Capitão Wagner), por não possuir mulheres concorrendo nos principais cargos tanto do Legislativo quanto do Executivo.

"Quero chamar atenção para a importância política que nós estamos vivendo no Brasil, no Estado do Ceará. Colocar também que você tenha muita tranquilidade para você analisar as propostas, escolher quem vai melhor representar, tanto no governo do Estado, na presidência da República e no Senado Federal. Importante lembrar que são dois votos para o Senado, ou seja, a gente vota duas vezes para o Senado Federal. Nós estamos colocando o nosso nome com o número 180, estamos fazendo uma parceria importante com o senador Cid Gomes, que é candidato à reeleição do Senado, com o número 400, esperando que o Estado do Ceará dê o seu recado e que a gente possa lamentar profundamente que os candidatos ligados ao partido do PL, o partido do Jair Bolsonaro, não tenham comparecido aqui ao debate para poder, inclusive, apresentar suas propostas para o eleitorado. Ou seja, se não dá satisfação agora, imagina depois de se eleger. Então, eu quero que o Ceará todo vote e vote 180 e 400 para o Senado."

"Parabenizar o Sistema Verdes Mares, o G1, pela sua iniciativa. Agradecer aqui à nossa companheira, Luizianne Lins. Dizer que no Brasil, hoje, são dois times. A gente não tem muitas opções. Ou você está no time do Bolsonaro, que a meu juízo fez muito mal ao país, ou você está no time do Lula. Nós aqui, a Luizianne, eu, o Elmano, nossos candidatos a deputados federais, estamos no time do presidente Lula. E daí é importante que a gente vote em pessoas que estejam atreladas, vinculadas, sejam defensoras desse projeto. Nós vamos ter uma eleição em que você vai votar em deputado federal, é o seu primeiro voto. Deputado estadual é o seu segundo voto. Como lembrou aqui a Luizianne, são dois votos para o Senado. Se você gosta da Luizianne, não tem problema. Vote nela e pode votar em mim também. E dessa forma a gente vai estar colocando no Senado duas pessoas que vão defender o Ceará."

articles.title: Xavier Becerra has the opportunity to ban executions in California once and for all
articles.summary: If GovGavin Newsom doesn’t issue a mass clemency, Becerra should. And now is the time for him to make that clear to California’s voters.
articles.body:
When it comes to the death penalty, California seems to be stuck. Capital punishment is still legal, and people are still receiving death sentences.

Since 1978, according to the Pacific Research Center, the state has imposed the death penalty in 769 cases. There have been 13 executions and six exonerations. Nearly 200 condemned have died waiting for execution.

No one has been executed in the Golden State since 2006, when Clarence Allen was put to death by lethal injection.

In a death penalty state, two decades is a long time to go without any executions. And, at the moment, there is no prospect that any of the more than 500 people awaiting execution will meet that fate any time soon. That is because Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) imposed a moratorium on executions in 2019. Moreover, the state has neither an approved execution protocol nor a functioning execution chamber.

California finds itself trapped between two competing impulses. “Voters reject efforts to end the death penalty and juries continue to authorize death sentences,” the Pacific Research Center observes , “while its governors are refusing to carry them out.”

On Sept. 8, Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for governor and Newsom’s likely successor, announced that if he is elected, he would also refuse to allow anyone to be executed. That decision is to be applauded.

Becerra has come a long way in his thinking about capital punishment. He was once vocal in his support of it. Should he become governor, Becerra will need to do more to get California out of its death penalty limbo. In announcing his intention to continue Newsom’s moratorium, he has laid the groundwork.

Becerra said that capital punishment is “a costly, flawed system that disproportionately impacts Black and brown communities and too often gets it wrong.” In fact, Black defendants are 8.7 times more likely be sentenced to death than others. The figure for Latino defendants is 6.2 times more likely to receive a death sentence.

The victim’s race also makes a big difference ; cases with a white victim are nearly 9 times more likely to result in a death sentence.

In the last 45 years, when it sentenced someone to death, California has gotten it wrong eight times . All of the men exonerated and released from California’s death row are people of color.

Becerra should call on the citizens of California to make sure that no one ever again be subject to such an imperfect system.

If that is a bridge too far, Becerra should commit himself to working with the legislature on “narrowing the scope of capital punishment” and “applying the state’s Racial Justice Act retroactively” to people who were sentenced to death before it was enacted in 2020.

Unlike in many other states, the California legislature cannot abolish its state’s death penalty. That is because it was approved by voters almost 50 years ago. And in two statewide referenda, one in 2012, the other in 2016, a majority of voters chose to retain it.

Despite the fact that surveys now show that most Californians prefer life in prison without parole to the death penalty, there is not much talk among abolitionists of trying a third time. Instead, efforts to end the death penalty in California have shifted from the ballot box to the courthouse.

Death penalty opponents are hoping to persuade the California Supreme Court to find that capital punishment violates the state constitution because it is applied in a racially discriminatory manner. The plaintiffs argue that under the state constitution, “proof of intentional discrimination is not required to advance an equal protection claim.” Instead, “a facially neutral statute’s disparate impact or discriminatory effect is sufficient to demonstrate a state equal protection violation.”

The state Supreme Court has already ordered a lower court to hold an evidentiary hearing for the purpose of examining the statistical evidence being offered to prove discrimination. And, as The Washington Post says , “It’s the first time a state’s death penalty statute has been challenged on systemic grounds untethered to an individual case, potentially paving a new legal pathway for capital punishment opponents in other states.”

That’s why Becerra should speak out in support of this litigation and fully embrace the abolitionist cause. In addition, he should also call on Newsom to commute all existing death sentences in his state before he leaves office.

Such an act, The Marshall Project claims , “would have a profound effect on capital punishment in the United States, slashing the total number of people under a death sentence across the country by more than a quarter. It would vastly outstrip similar moves by other governors and even President Joe Biden, who commuted 37 death sentences on his way out of office.”

If Newsom doesn’t issue a mass clemency, Becerra should. And now is the time for him to make that clear to California’s voters.

Austin Sarat is the William Nelson Cromwell Professor of Jurisprudence and Political Science at Amherst College.

articles.title: Down but not out: How America can rebuild after Trump
articles.summary: The Trump presidency has been an exhausting crisis-a-day affair, profoundly damaging to the American spirit and its mission in the world. The crises will continue. But some good will come from them if we buckle up for the rough road ahead, recommit to that spirit, and unite to fix the damage democracy has endured.
articles.body:
There’s good news and bad news as we approach the midterm elections.

The good news is that Democrats have a realistic opportunity to win control of at least one house of Congress. The bad news is that it won’t make much difference in President Trump’s behavior. We are likely to have a rough election followed by another contentious two years of his presidency. Even with control of Congress, Democrats will not be able to leash Trump.

First, we need to get through the midterms, despite Trump’s efforts to undermine confidence in the outcome. If Democrats win back the House, they can impeach Trump on any number of transgressions. But it would be merely performative unless two-thirds of the Senate agrees to convict and remove him from office. Two previous impeachments have not changed Trump’s behavior — there is no reason to think a third would, either.

If Democrats win control of both houses of Congress, they will be able to pass legislation to proscribe Trump’s abuses of power, but he would veto the bills. Democrats are unlikely to acquire the supermajorities necessary to override his vetoes. And although Congress has the leverage of the federal budget, Trump has shown he largely disregards it .

Short of Trump resigning out of boredom, poor health or crimes that even MAGA can’t tolerate, we can expect more of the domestic and international abuses we have seen in the last two years.

Yet as painful as this is, Trump is unintentionally teaching us important lessons about the American experiment and what happens when we elect leaders who embody our worst impulses rather than our highest principles. Even the divinely endowed rights in the Constitution are not immune when we give corrupt people political power. Elections matter a lot.

Many on the right believe that Trump’s presidency has been ordained . They may be correct. We Americans apparently needed to learn these lessons, and Trump is uniquely qualified to teach them. “The depths of his dishonesty is just astounding to me,” Trump’s former chief of staff Gen. John Kelly observed . “He is the most flawed person I have ever met in my life.”

The challenge for the rest of us, citizen and elected official alike, is to turn the negatives of the Trump era into something positive. At the grassroots, this means giving some grace to those who voted for Trump. Who among us has never been fooled or misled? We need to come back together for the work ahead.

In Congress, Democrats promise to hold Trump accountable if they win one or both houses. This means endless investigations and hearings that keep picking at the scabs of democracy’s wounds. Investigations and hearings should focus not on political theater, but on exposing the reforms to better protect democracy and the rule of law. The objective would be to fix what Trump has revealed about weaknesses in the Constitution, our laws, the system of checks and balances, and the guardrails against corruption.

Over the next two years, Congress should build an agenda not only to repair the weaknesses and damages, but also to build government back better, including constraints on presidential power for Republicans and Democrats alike. The ideal would be a bipartisan legislative agenda for the president and Congress we elect in 2028.

This agenda — a Project 2028 for the everyman — could fix the holes in the Voting Rights Act, address the “major questions” issue to strengthen EPA’s authority for nationwide environmental protection, and reinstitute the most important of the hundreds of environmental rules Trump’s people have rescinded. Congress should make the endangerment finding on greenhouse gas emissions a matter of law instead of EPA’s discretion. It should clarify questions about domestic military deployments and the constitutional rights of immigrants .

Congress should create an enforceable ethics code and term limits for Supreme Court justices, protect the Department of Justice from improper political influence, develop presidential ethics rules, and prohibit private profiteering from public office. It should craft a carefully defined package of constitutional amendments to reform campaign finance, prevent abuses of presidential pardon power, and overturn the Supreme Court’s ruling that presidents cannot be prosecuted for violating the law while performing official duties.

The Trump presidency has been an exhausting crisis-a-day affair, profoundly damaging to the American spirit and its mission in the world. The crises will continue. But some good will come from them if we buckle up for the rough road ahead, recommit to that spirit, and unite to fix the damage democracy has endured.

William S. Becker is co-editor of and a contributor to “ Democracy Unchained: How to Rebuild Government for the People,” and a contributor to “ Democracy in a Hotter Time .” He previously served as a senior official in the Wisconsin Department of Justice. He is currently executive director of the Presidential Climate Action Project.

articles.title: CNN, Politico, MS NOW sue Trump administration over White House ban
articles.summary: Trump says ban targets ‘fake news’, which poses a ‘threat to our National Security’.
articles.body:
Leading news outlets CNN, Politico and MS NOW have sued the ⁠⁠administration of United States President Donald Trump after it banned them from the White House grounds.

“This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes,” the outlets said in a joint statement on Monday.

Later on Monday, their complaint was filed in the Washington, DC, federal court.

The White House revoked the credentials of the journalists of the organisations “without notice or process” because it “objected to our reporting”, their statement said. “Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.”

All three outlets said on Saturday that their journalists were turned away from the White House grounds and their press credentials confiscated.

In the statement, they added that they would file ⁠⁠a lawsuit in the US District Court for the District of Columbia and could see emergency hearings in the case as soon as this week.

Also on Monday, leading US broadcasters, ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC said in a joint statement that they suspended TV “pool” coverage of Trump. TV broadcasters rotate responsibility for filming the president at some events.

“The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organisation because it objects to its reporting,” the statement said.

Later on Monday, US Vice President JD Vance defended the ban, saying it was not an attack on free speech as the affected media organisations could still report on Trump, get the public reports and talk to people in the administration.

“What the president has said is, we’re not going to give you special access inside the White House,” Vance said, claiming that the move was against “propaganda”.

“We have to remember those three outlets account about 92 percent of the stories that they have on the President of the United States on the administration are negative,” he said. “That’s not representative of the American people. It’s not representative of public opinion. So if you’re going to engage in what is effectively far left propaganda. Why would a Republican White House give you special access?”

Trump said on Friday he was banning the outlets from the presidential mansion as punishment for distributing what he called “fake news”.

He did not detail what prompted the ban but on Monday said it was not an attack on the free press, “which I cherish”, but “an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America”.

“It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control,” he wrote on Truth Social. “It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”

The White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA) called on the Trump administration to immediately restore access to the three outlets.

“The implications extend beyond these organisations: a standard used to exclude one news outlet because of its coverage could be applied to any outlet in the future,” WHCA president Jacqui Heinrich said in a statement on X.

“The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinise those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favourably.”

The Trump administration has been denying access to many ⁠⁠leading news organisations while elevating new media outlets seen ⁠⁠as more sympathetic to the administration. He has also filed a number of lawsuits against media giants, including The New York Times and CBS.

The move comes as his fellow Republicans seek to defend their narrow majorities in Congress in the November midterm elections. Pre-election opinion polls suggest the public is souring on Republicans and Trump’s approval ⁠⁠ratings are at near historic lows.

articles.title: GOP fiscal hawk sounds alarm on 'out of control' federal spending, saying 'both parties have failed us'
articles.summary: Sen. Paul, who said "both parties have failed us," does not support President Trump's proposal to dole out $5,000 to American adults if the GOP wins both chambers in the midterms.
articles.body: With the U.S. national debt soaring above $40 trillion and the federal government engaging in massive deficit spending, Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky. — a fiscal hawk who says the situation is "out of control" and "both parties have failed us" — does not support President Donald Trump's proposal to dole out $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans win both chambers of Congress during the midterms. The president floated the idea during a speech earlier this month at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, calling it "the Trump dividend." Asked about the president's proposal during an interview on Thursday, Paul told Fox News Digital that he is not in favor of giving away "dividends when there's a deficit." "We're running $2 trillion dollars short," he said, noting that he "can't imagine giving out money when you're running a deficit." Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment on Friday. RAND PAUL CLASHES WITH FELLOW REPUBLICAN OVER AI 'KILL SWITCH' AS SENATE GRAPPLES WITH 'TERMINATOR' FEARS America's soaring national debt has surpassed the staggering sum of $40 trillion and shows no signs of stopping. "And so, the debt is very important. So it's not just important that it might bankrupt us or overwhelm us in some kinda crisis in the future," Paul said, acknowledging that as "a possibility. But every day you're being hurt by it because it's stealing the value" of people's earnings, he indicated. "So it is literally out of control," Paul said. "And really both parties have failed us because both parties are afraid to tell the American public that some things they like from government would have to be reduced when we cut costs." Paul has a plan that he says would balance the budget through a series of spending cuts over five years. GOP LAWMAKERS PUMP BRAKES ON TRUMP'S $5K CHECK PROMISE: 'WHERE ARE YOU GETTING THE MONEY?' "Now when I first introduced it, it was a 1% cut, or a one-penny plan, and you cut spending 1% a year for five years, and with economic growth increasing revenue, the lines cross at about five years," balancing the budget, he explained. "Well, when COVID came along, both parties frankly started passin' out money like drunken sailors and... the deficit ballooned. Now to balance the budget in five years it's called the six-penny plan cuz it takes about a 6% cut. But it still shows you that we wouldn't have to eliminate everything." While the cuts under his proposal would not apply to Social Security, they would apply to Medicare, he indicated, though he suggested it could be possible "to cut Medicare 6% without cutting any health benefits," saying that he thinks there is a lot of "waste and fraud in" the program. He also suggested that additional means testing could be used to achieve the Medicare spending cuts. Paul — who ran for president in 2016 but dropped out after placing fifth in the Iowa GOP presidential caucuses — is considering throwing his hat into the ring again. "I'd say we're 50-50," he said. "I do think that there should be a candidate on the Republican side, at least, who believes that international trade is good for our country and good for the economy, that believes in free markets, that isn't a big believer in big government coming in and managing contracts and owning parts of countries, that isn't a believer in giving out money we don't have." RAND PAUL SAYS HE'S '50-50' ON RUNNING FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028, 'THINKING ABOUT IT' CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Paul said he does not "want there to be a choice of four populists running for president," noting that he wants there to be "at least one free-market candidate. I could be that, or maybe somebody else could be," he said, indicating that he will decide after the midterm elections.

articles.title: DHS now leading investigation into shooting involving ICE officer in Austin
articles.summary: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said Monday its investigations unit is now leading the investigation into a shooting in Austin, Texas, over the weekend that involved a federal immigration officer. The DHS said in a statement its Homeland Security Investigations agency is leading the probe into the incident. An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)…
articles.body:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said Monday its investigations unit is now leading the investigation into a shooting in Austin, Texas, over the weekend that involved a federal immigration officer.

The DHS said in a statement its Homeland Security Investigations agency is leading the probe into the incident.

An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in the Texas capital on Sunday shot Venezuelan national Wilber Rafael Garces Perez. The man, 28, “illegally entered” the U.S. during the Biden administration and “had a final order of removal” from an immigration judge, according to the department.

Garces Perez was shot in the torso, local authorities said. His condition as of early Monday was “stable,” per the DHS — which added he was “in federal custody pending removal.”

The shooting sparked protests in Austin, a city with a heavy concentration of Hispanics. Nationwide demonstrations also erupted earlier this year after federal immigration officers fatally shot two U.S. citizens in Minnesota, Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

Austin Mayor Kirk Watson (D) told reporters Sunday that the city’s police department should be involved in the investigation to provide “clear, third-party eyes,” according to The Associated Press .

City police officers were not involved in the operation or the shooting of Garces Perez, Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis told reporters, the AP reported.

“ICE shot Wilber Rafael Garces Perez in Austin. He’s been taken out of the hospital and into ICE custody,” Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), whose district includes part of Austin, wrote Sunday on the social platform X.

“If ICE deports him, the key witness to their shooting disappears,” Casar added. “He must not be removed from this country, and he must receive proper medical care.”

articles.title: Inflation and tariffs shake Republican-leaning states in the Midwest
articles.summary: A Democratic challenger is running neck-and-neck with Republican incumbent Roger Marshall in the Kansas U.S. Senate race, reflecting broader national discontent with the Trump administration’s economic policies and local controversies surrounding Marshall’s medical debt collection practices.
articles.body:
Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in more than 90 years . But this year a Democrat is running neck-and-neck with an incumbent Republican.

What is happening? The quick answer is that the Republicans have a bad candidate.

The longer answer is that 2026 shows signs of being a bad year for any Republican. That includes Republicans in solidly Republican, midwestern states such as Kansas, Nebraska and Iowa.

Discontent with inflation will spread across regional lines when 63 percent of all voters, including 73 percent of Independents agree, in a Fox poll last week , that “the Trump administration has made the economy worse.”

The poll found 62 percent of Americans say buying groceries is now a “major problem,” and 61 percent said the price of gas is a “major problem.”

And there’s more: In the last year, voters have become even more negative on President Trump’s use of tariffs that fuel inflation and economic chaos. Opposition has grown by 7 percentage points to 64 percent.

Political alarm is now at the level that Decision Desk HQ gives the Democrats a 70 percent chance of winning the House and a 52 percent chance of winning the Senate.

Another flashing red light last week was news of Vice President Vance traveling to Kansas to campaign for the Republican incumbent. Two recent polls show the Democrat in the Kansas Senate race within five percentage points or with a one-point lead.

The Republicans’ problem in Kansas is exacerbated by damning reports about their candidate, Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.). At a Kansas State Fair debate Marshall was loudly booed when he tried to defend having sued patients , including mothers of newborn babies, for as little as $100 in unpaid bills. Many of the people sued by Marshall, an OB-GYN doctor, live in a rural Kansas county, Barton, which has a high rate of poverty.

“I had every intention to pay, I was just struggling,” one of Marshall’s patients, Kellie Clutts, told reporters . Marshall sued Clutts in 2015 over a $129 bill stemming from a postpartum visit shortly after her daughter’s birth.

In the face of jeers from the crowd at the state fair, Marshall defended his medical-debt collection practices as “common business practices.” The booing did not stop.

This story has added power, given that Marshall makes his opposition to abortion and Christian faith essential to his political identity.

Even some of Marshall’s fellow Republicans have turned against him. Former Kansas Gov. Bill Graves (R) endorsed the Democrat running against Marshall.

“For the last six years, Senator Roger Marshall has turned his back on Kansas,” Graves said in endorsing Marshall’s opponent, Adam Hamilton, a United Methodist pastor and Democrat. “In contrast [to Marhsall], Adam Hamilton stands as a bulwark of kindness, humility and service to others.”

Adding to the problem is Marshall’s record of support for “One Big Beautiful Bill.” President Trump’s signature legislation has reduced federal Medicaid spending. The result in Kansas, and around the country, has been increased financial pressure on rural hospitals, 40 percent of which lose money .

“You’ve got to have courage,” Hamilton said in criticizing Marshall’s decision to back Trump’s bill . “And courage is when you stand up to your president and your party, and you say, ‘This is hurting people back home.’ And you say it even if your president’s going to bully you, pick on you, primary you and call you names. You still say, ‘This is not OK.'”

Trump’s tariffs are yet another problem for Marshall. They are driving up prices for farmers while hurting sales.

The same is true in other Midwest states where Republicans find themselves tossed in this year’s political tornado.

In neighboring Nebraska, Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts (R) is fighting to survive a challenge from an independent candidate, Dan Osborn. Ricketts, whose wealthy family built TD Ameritrade and owns the Chicago Cubs, is also seeing inflation and tariffs sinking his chances.

His opponent, Osborn, is running as an independent to avoid damage from Trump attacking Democrats as “communists.” Recent polling has shown a competitive race.

Put it all together, and this big storm is picking up speed from tariffs hitting an already stressed agricultural economy, strong challengers emerging, an unpopular president and wealthy, Republican incumbents facing populist anger.

You could see some of those pressures last week in House races in Iowa. Republican Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, both representing competitive districts, broke with Trump and most of their own party to support legislation aimed at ending U.S. military involvement in Iran . Both cited the war’s costs, including its effects on their constituents and the farm economy.

Where does the storm take us? Will Democrats and independents make serious inroads in Great Plains states that Trump carried three times?

Kansas will provide the most fascinating test. Like Dorothy in “The Wizard of Oz,” Democrats would love to find their way back home to Kansas. Will America soon awake to a Democrat winning a U.S. Senate seat from Kansas for the first time since 1932? We will know in less than 50 days.

Juan Williams is senior political analyst for Fox News Channel and a prize-winning civil rights historian. He is the author of the new book “ New Prize for These Eyes: The Rise of America’s Second Civil Rights Movement . “

Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) in Nebraska, Kennedy acknowledged the war has resulted in price increases for oil and fertilizer. But the Louisiana Republican argued the U.S. has so far…
articles.body:
Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) predicted Sunday the U.S. will be “out of” Iran in six months , as the conflict approaches the seven-month mark.

While stumping for Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) in Nebraska, Kennedy acknowledged the war has resulted in price increases for oil and fertilizer. But the Louisiana Republican argued the U.S. has so far been successful against Tehran, adding that economic relief is coming for Americans.

“We’re achieving our objectives in Iran, and without going into details, I think we’ll be out of there in about six months,” Kennedy remarked. “And when that happens, you’re going to see the price of oil go down, and you’re going to see inflation go down.”

The GOP senator added that if voters elect Ricketts and other Republican lawmakers, the federal government will enact policies to “get the cost of living to go down.”

The Iran conflict , which President Trump initially said would end in roughly a month, has passed the six-month mark with no public signs of a deal to end hostilities. The president said Thursday he was weighing whether to “annihilate” the Islamic Republic’s regime or not.

“It’s a big decision. Anything could happen with me,” Trump told Axios .

During the war, the president has threatened to strike civilian infrastructure in Iran and even warned the entire Iranian civilization “will die.” Such actions would qualify as war crimes under international law.

The House last week passed a third war powers resolution to limit Trump’s military authority against Iran, with the number of GOP lawmakers voting in favor of the measure rising from four to seven .

The president and administration officials have argued, though, that the War Powers Act is unconstitutional .

The conflict has come with economic consequences for Americans, particularly at the pump, as gas prices have spiked as a result of the Iranian military restricting shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

The national average price of regular gas is roughly $4.48 per gallon as of Monday, according to AAA . That is about 37 cents higher than a month ago and roughly $1.50 greater than two days before the U.S. and Israel launched the war.

The cost of the war itself has also risen. The Pentagon told Congress on Aug. 13 that the conflict’s price tag had increased from $37.5 billion in July to $42 billion, a congressional aide told The Hill.

articles.summary: Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) says Donald Trump Jr.’s acceptance of lavish gifts from a Russian oligarch with ties to the Kremlin looks “really bad” and warned it would be “wrong” for anyone with “proximity to power” to accept items of great value from an ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin. “Anytime someone gives you a…
articles.body:
Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) says Donald Trump Jr.’s acceptance of lavish gifts from a Russian oligarch with ties to the Kremlin looks “really bad” and warned it would be “wrong” for anyone with “proximity to power” to accept items of great value from an ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“Anytime someone gives you a $250,000 gift and they have strong ties to the Kremlin, that’s wrong,” Cassidy told Margaret Brennan, the host of CBS’s “ Face the Nation ,” on Sunday.

“You — with that proximity to power, being the president’s son, you’ve got to give faith to the American people that Washington is not a swamp,” he added. “And even though in your mind it might be a gift, the appearance of it is really bad.”

Cassidy, however, said Trump Jr., President Trump’s eldest son, made the right move by paying back Russian businessman Umar Kremlev.

“And so I’m glad it’s been repaid,” he said. “It would be nice to have that kind of verified, and, no, it shouldn’t have been done in the first place.”

Cassidy became at least the third Republican senator to criticize Trump Jr.’s acceptance of tens of thousands of dollars’ worth of gifts from Kremlev, the president of the International Boxing Association, who helped pay for a luxurious after-wedding party for Trump Jr. and his new wife Bettina Trump.

ProPublica broke the story last week that Kremlev paid to rent one of two private islands where the Trumps held a three-day party in the Bahamas and also footed the bill for a private fireworks show.

Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) on Friday ripped Trump Jr. for taking such lavish gifts from a Kremlin ally, declaring it smelled of “corruption.”

“A Russian oligarch paid for a lavish wedding after-party for Donald Trump Jr., which to me just thinks, ‘It’s corruption,’ I don’t like it,” Curtis said in a video Friday.

“You’ll hear more from me later on. This is a big deal,” he said.

Bettina Trump confirmed in a social media post that the couple’s “dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations” but emphasized it was “AFTER” the wedding itself, which was a private ceremony attended only by family.

President Trump told reporters Friday that his son paid back Kremlev and that he did nothing wrong.

“Well, it’s totally allowed, and a lot of people have parties and all, but it’s totally allowed,” the president said. “But as I understand it, he paid him back. He didn’t want to have that, so I hear he paid him back.”

articles.title: Brainwashed by fear: How to save 2 generations lost to climate panic
articles.summary: For more than four decades, Americans have been subjected to a relentless drumbeat of environmental doom. They have been terrified by warnings of acid rain, the ozone hole, melting ice caps, drowned coastal cities, superstorms and mass extinctions. Then came Al Gore and increasingly apocalyptic warnings about global warming, which has since been rebranded as…
articles.body:
For more than four decades, Americans have been subjected to a relentless drumbeat of environmental doom. They have been terrified by warnings of acid rain, the ozone hole, melting ice caps, drowned coastal cities, superstorms and mass extinctions. Then came Al Gore and increasingly apocalyptic warnings about global warming, which has since been rebranded as “climate change.”

Today, we can see the consequences. Two generations of young people have been taught not to respect the environment, but rather to fear the future.

The numbers are disturbing. A Lancet Planetary Health survey of 15,793 Americans ages 16 to 25 found that 85 percent were at least moderately worried about climate change, including 58 percent who were very or extremely worried. More than half said climate change made them hesitant to have children .

Other research points the same way. A review of multiple studies found that stronger climate worry lines up with wanting fewer children or none at all.

Think about that. We have convinced millions of young people that the future is so bleak that they should reconsider having children.

Yet the picture of a dying planet bears little resemblance to the measurable world around us.

The Earth is getting greener. NASA reported that 25 to 50 percent of the world’s vegetated land greened significantly between 1982 and 2015 — an increase in leaf area roughly twice the size of the continental U.S. Researchers attributed about 70 percent of that greening to rising carbon dioxide.

So carbon dioxide is not merely an emission — it is plant food.

Agriculture tells the same story. The world now grows nearly three times as much grain on the same acre as it did in 1961. The cropland saved is close to the area of the U.S. and India combined. Credit better seeds, machinery, irrigation, modern farming, fossil fuel-derived fertilizer, and that carbon dioxide boost.

Our air is cleaner, too. EPA reports that emissions of the six main air pollutants fell 79 percent between 1970 and 2024, even as the economy grew 338 percent, Americans drove 195 percent more miles, and the population grew by two-thirds.

Prosperity has surged as well. The number of people living in extreme poverty worldwide fell from roughly 2.3 billion in 1990 to about 800 million today, even as the world population grew by nearly three billion. Life expectancy , literacy, and living standards are at record highs.

We have heard the doom and gloom predictions before. Paul Ehrlich’s 1968 bestseller, “The Population Bomb,” promised mass starvation in the 1970s. Instead, Norman Borlaug’s Green Revolution fed a billion more people. Being wrong has never slowed down the doomsayers.

None of this means environmental problems are imaginary. It means they are problems to solve and not reasons to surrender.

Previous generations built dams, cured diseases, split the atom, crossed oceans, and landed men on the Moon. They faced world wars, depressions, and nuclear standoffs, real existential dangers. Their answer was not to stop having children. It was to build a better world for them.

Even Elon Musk, who believes strongly that man-made carbon dioxide threatens the climate, preaches innovation and expansion — not retreat and despair. That is the mindset young people need.

So teach the real problems we can do something about — not false climate doom. Teach the triumphs, not just the panic. Teach how human ingenuity cleaned our air and rivers, tripled crop yields, cut extreme poverty by two-thirds, and greened a massive share of the planet.

Parents, this one is on us. Ask your school district what your children are being taught about climate, and what they are not. Ask to see the curriculum. Ask whether a single one of these numbers appears in it. Then say so out loud at the next school board meeting.

Two generations have been taught to fear the future. Let’s teach the next one to build it.

Frank Lasee is a senior policy analyst with the Committee For A Constructive Tomorrow .

articles.title: Omar's new legislation targeting ICE sparks outrage when the internet sees what's in it: 'Un-American'
articles.summary: Ilhan Omar's Make ICE Pay Act would redirect nearly $140 billion in ICE and Border Patrol funding to communities impacted by immigration enforcement.
articles.body:
Rep. Ilhan Omar introduced legislation to redirect over $100 billion in funds from immigration enforcement to communities impacted by DHS operations.

The Make ICE Pay Act proposed by Omar would send nearly $140 billion of ICE and Border Patrol funding to local recovery efforts across the country.

Conservatives have criticized the bill, calling it un-American and emblematic of an ideology that prioritizes protecting illegal immigrants over enforcing immigration law.

Conservatives are pushing back after Rep. Ilhan Omar. D-Minn., introduced legislation that would redirect over $100 billion in funds previously allocated to immigration enforcement and "invest it into communities across the country that have been impacted by the Department of Homeland Security's heinous operations."

Omar explained in a press release Thursday that her Make ICE Pay Act is a response to "Operation Metro Surge" in Minnesota and that it would send nearly $140 billion of ICE and Border Patrol funding from Trump's signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act toward "local recovery efforts" from immigration enforcement that has taken place across the country.

Omar says the funding will be used by local jurisdictions to provide economic relief and distribute money through the states to nonprofits, small businesses and other impacted entities to support schools, healthcare and psychological services, increased local-government expenses, investigations and memorialization efforts. The program would be administered by the Department of Housing and Urban Development, overseen by its inspector general and expire three years after its creation.

"ICE has been tearing through our nation, devastating our neighborhoods, our cities, and our businesses," Omar posted on X about the legislation. "Our communities deserve accountability. My Make ICE Pay Act will redirect ICE's $140 billion budget to the communities they've hurt the most."

While the bill's future is bleak as long as Republicans control Congress and the White House, it was quickly blasted by conservatives as emblematic of an ideology that places more of an emphasis on protecting illegal immigrants than it does enforcing immigration law.

"This bill is un-American," Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., posted on X . "This bill defunds law enforcement and gives their funding to the communities harboring criminal illegal aliens. Democrats fight for everyone except the American people."

"The definition of America last," conservative influencer account LibsofTikTok posted on X . "Denaturalize and deport."

"Defund ICE. Weaken the border. Then expect safer communities? That math isn't mathing," Arkansas Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders posted on X.

"Her entire existence is on crippling the United States," Republican John Nagel, running against Omar in Minnesota's 5th Congressional District this November, posted on X . "She is anti-police and pro communism."

Fox News Digital reached out to Omar's office for comment.

White House border czar Tom Homan confirmed to Fox News last week that the Department of Homeland Security is looking into allegations involving Omar, but would not disclose details about what he described as an "ongoing criminal investigation."

Pressed on whether the federal government has evidence that Omar committed immigration or naturalization fraud , Homan declined to comment.

When subsequently asked directly whether he was confirming an investigation involving Omar , Homan replied, "I'm confirming that ICE is, yeah — look, I said months ago that there's something that's been reported and needs to be looked at."

Omar has long been dogged by allegations that she married a man that critics allege is her brother as part of an immigration scheme. Omar has repeatedly denied the allegation, and the claim has not been proven in public records. In December, she dismissed the claims as "bigoted lies," writing on social media that Trump was obsessed with her.

Fox News Digital's Max Bacall contributed to this report

articles.title: Trump’s $5,000 check is definitely not in the mail — but your ballot could be
articles.summary: Unfortunately, the effort to hinder mail-in voting is only part of the Trump administration’s broader efforts to rig the midterm elections in favor of Republicans.
articles.body:
In a necessary and unquestionably correct decision , the U.S. Supreme Court last week declined to let President Trump throw the midterm elections into chaos with his scheme to use the U.S. Postal Service to interfere with mail-in voting.

The ruling should have been unanimous. Several states had already mailed out ballots . Others had already printed their election materials. And the Postal Service had not even created the portal that states were supposed to use to upload lists of citizens that, according to Trump’s unconstitutional order, would be used to decide which ballots to deliver.

It is appalling that Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas were willing to let the Trump administration impose last-minute changes that were sure to cause what both Republican and Democratic election officials warned would be massive disruption and voter disenfranchisement.

The court’s MAGA maximalists seem to be operating under the principle that anything that interferes with Trump’s authoritarian whims is a violation of the Constitution. Fortunately, in this case, even Trump justices who helped invent king-like immunity for the president recognized that the attempt to force new election rules on the states — especially this close to an election — was a recipe for disaster.

Trump responded in the highly reasonable and presidential fashion for which he is known, ranting angrily about the justices he nominated, charging that they have given into bullying by the “ Radical Left ” and are now “ merely a shell of their original selves .”

Unfortunately, the effort to hinder mail-in voting is only part of the Trump administration’s broader efforts to rig the midterm elections in favor of Republicans.

After the 2020 election and its aftermath, we know that Trump and his supporters are willing to try just about anything to overturn the results of elections they lose. Today, with the president’s unpopularity dragging down Republican prospects for keeping control of Congress, Trump is sowing doubt that the elections will be fair. He claims, as he has before, that Democrats cannot possibly win unless they cheat.

In August, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin signaled another potential avenue of attack, warning that Chinese-made components in election machines pose “significant security risks.” Given that Trump and his allies have repeatedly made wild false claims about the 2020 election involving foreign governments and overseas servers and a mysterious “algorithm” that supposedly flipped votes from Trump to Biden, it’s not hard to imagine the kind of disinformation they could be preparing to spread about voting machines to challenge the outcome of elections this fall.

Fortunately, we know what we’re up against. We have seen the Trump team in action. We will not be surprised by any skullduggery they attempt before, on, or after Election Day. Election officials, voting rights groups, and legal organizations are on full alert.

Trump is the biggest threat to local officials’ ability to conduct an election whose outcome can be accepted by Americans of all political stripes as fairly reflecting the will of the voters. And we approach these consequential elections at a time when Trump’s behavior is increasingly erratic and his rhetoric divorced from reality .

That is the context for his latest ploy to keep Congress in the hands of subservient Republicans who will never hold him accountable for corruption or anything else. At their recent convention, Trump promised $5,000 to every to every American adult if Republicans keep control of both houses of Congress.

His dangled bribe is about as credible as the bogus defenses and justifications offered by administration officials who cannot contradict the boss. His claim that he could promise the more than $1 trillion bribe because the country is “ making so much money ” is laughable in the face of the multi-trillion-dollar deficit his administration is already running.

Few people believe Trump — and nobody should. He promised Americans thousands of dollars in Department of Government Efficiency and tariff dividends. American families never got those checks. Instead, they got higher gas prices and a higher cost of living that are the direct result of Trump’s reckless policies.

Instead of changing directions in ways that might actually help people, Trump is throwing out a false promise of cash. It reeks of desperation and dishonesty.

I think, and polling suggests, it’s getting less likely that voters will keep the country on its current destructive path based on trust-me bluster from our self-proclaimed “ high IQ ” president. Americans know Trump’s $5,000 check is not in the mail. It will never be in the mail. But now that Trump’s plans to disrupt voting have been rejected, our ballots may be.

Whether you plan to cast your ballot by mail, place it in a drop box, vote early in person or go to your polling place on Election Day, Nov. 3. Be sure to vote — for accountability, affordability, the beginning of the end of the Trump regime’s chokehold on our country and the chance to build a future where all our people, all our families and all our communities can thrive.

Svante Myrick is president of People For the American Way .

articles.summary: Cory Booker seemed to dismiss Abdul El-Sayed as a "fringe" figure on "Meet the Press," but their recent "warm" D.C. meeting tells a very different story.
articles.body: Sen. Cory Booker’s response to a question about Abdul El-Sayed’s election campaign in Michigan has some online observers questioning whether the Democratic Party’s elected officials are behind the socialist-adjacent candidate. The Democrat from New Jersey joined Kristen Welker on ABC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday, when he was asked a wide variety of policy questions along with a question about President Donald Trump's announcement that he is banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House grounds. But the question about El-Sayed stole the show. "Senator, you see there in our polls that socialism is viewed even more negatively than the 'MAGA movement,'" Welker began. "President Trump is trying to paint progressives, and frankly all Democrats, as socialists, and we're seeing one of the big battles play out for progressivism in Michigan right now with Abdul El-Sayed... do you think Democrats are drawing a firm enough line between themselves and socialism?" MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE ENDORSED BY AOC AND BERNIE SANDERS INSISTS HE'S NOT A SOCIALIST "Again, this is really what the Republicans want to do — focus on a few fringe people," Booker replied. He then diverted away from discussing the party establishment's fracture with far-left candidates and pivoted to attacking Trump's economic and foreign policies. "I serve in the United States Senate and I could go through my colleagues, left and right," Booker said. "What we want right now is to end these reckless tariffs and drive down prices, to end this war to drive down prices, to give a tax plan for this country that puts more money in working peoples' pockets and ends the giveaways to the wealthiest of Americans." Political observers on X quickly seized on the response, claiming that Booker is too late in the push to try and distinguish the Democratic Party from its far-left fringe and the rise in socialist candidates in this year's midterm elections. "Oops," radio show host Jason Rantz said simply of Booker's comments to Welker. "A day late and a dollar short," said Trump Media & Technology Group communications adviser Katie Zacharia. "Senator Booker is trying to disassociate as the 'Big Tent' burns." She added that the senator should have condemned socialism outright, claiming the "Dem party [is] in disarray." SEE IT: DEM SENATORS RALLY BEHIND EL-SAYED BUT DUCK QUESTIONS ON PROGRESSIVE AGENDA "I really wonder what the internals they showed those senators in DC said," said author Carl Paulus, speculating that polling within the Democratic Party could suggest that the far left is dragging them down and causing sitting lawmakers to change their tune with just weeks until November's election. Booker was one of several senators who met with El-Sayed during a trip to Washington, D.C., last week. After the meeting, led by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., El-Sayed's campaign described the gathering as "warm." "We’re united in the fact that we have to win Michigan. Whatever our difference is, our agreement on the importance of winning Michigan to take back the Senate majority [is] overwhelming," El-Sayed told MS NOW of the meeting. "We had a warm meeting, good conversation, and I know that we left that conversation committed to doing what we need to do to take on different perspectives. And I also know that the things that bring us together are so much bigger than any of the disagreements that we have." articles.body:
Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) said Sunday that President Trump was “very receptive” to her warning to him about Hispanic voters over his administration’s immigration actions.

“He was a gentleman, very courteous, very receptive,” Salazar told CBS News’s Margaret Brennan on “Face the Nation” of her conversation with the president.

“And I told him exactly what you just repeated: ‘Sir, you have this — this moment in history where you can keep the pot of gold that you brought to the GOP in 2024. No other president.’ And you know I covered, for 35 years, Spanish television. No other president was able to convince the Hispanics to vote 55 points for a GOP president. Please preserve that fortune that you have brought to the party,” she added

Salazar alleged in a campaign advertisement released last week that the president had gone “too far” with federal immigration enforcement operations .

“The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” Salazar, who is currently running for reelection, said in the ad.

“You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism,” she added. “I’m not talking about giving them amnesty. I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land.”

The Trump administration has faced heat for its strict immigration agenda throughout Trump’s second term, and Republicans are facing a deficit of trust on the issue of immigration, according to recent polling ahead of this November’s key midterms.

Federal immigration authorities have also been involved in multiple deadly incidents during the current Trump administration, with the killings of two U.S. citizens in Minnesota earlier this year sparking mass outrage.

On Monday, the Department of Homeland Security said its investigations unit is leading the probe into a shooting in Austin, Texas, over the weekend that involved a federal immigration officer.

articles.title: Barrasso says ‘we need to do more’ on affordability as midterms near
articles.summary: Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) said Sunday that the GOP needs to “do more” to lower costs for Americans with the midterms roughly six weeks away. During an interview on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” Barrasso acknowledged that people “around the country are feeling the pain,” noting he has heard concerns from Wyoming ranchers and…
articles.body:
Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) said Sunday that the GOP needs to “do more” to lower costs for Americans with the midterms roughly six weeks away.

During an interview on NBC’s “ Meet the Press ,” Barrasso acknowledged that people “around the country are feeling the pain,” noting he has heard concerns from Wyoming ranchers and farmers.

“People vote about what’s going on in their life and their future,” he told host Kristen Welker. “And we know we need to do more. We need to get more money into people’s pockets.”

The senator later touted the GOP-backed One Big Beautiful Bill Act , which enshrined President Trump’s 2017 tax cuts and new deductions for overtime and tipped pay.

The six-plus-month war in Iran, though, has raised costs for Americans. Gas prices are approaching $4.50 per gallon on average, and annual inflation increased from 2.4 percent in February to 3.4 percent in August, as measured by the consumer price index.

More than 4 in 10 respondents to a recent Politico/Public First survey blamed Trump for the state of the economy , with 19 percent of Republicans and 70 percent of Democrats faulting him. Roughly 55 percent of respondents in an NBC News poll also said Trump’s policies worsened the economy .

One thing the federal government could do to lower costs is cutting regulations to allow for increased oil production, according to Barrasso.

“We need to do more with permitting,” the Wyoming Republican told Welker. “That’s legislation we’re working on now.”

Trump, meanwhile, has proposed sending $5,000 dividends to every American if Republicans maintain control of Congress in November. But multiple GOP lawmakers have warned about such an initiative’s impact on the growing national debt.

When Welker asked Barrasso whether he was committed to passing legislation to make that a reality, he deflected and said the president is “always looking for ways to get more money in people’s pockets.”

The senator added, “Bottom line is, the president is right to be focused on people and the economy. I’m focused on winning the House and winning the Senate.”

"This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," the three outlets said in a joint statement.
