articles.title: America’s politics of fear could finally be over
articles.summary: Following three decades of scaring each other to death, Americans are tired and longing for change.
articles.body:
In a fiery speech at the Republican Midterm Convention, Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) declared that this year’s crop of Democratic candidates was “extreme” — that should they gain power, they would “rip” the nation’s “heart out of our chests.”

His address was so virulent that the next morning, Rev. Al Sharpton asked his colleagues on Morning Joe to join hands while he prayed for divine intervention to calm the distraught senator.

Scott was not the only one to preach fire and brimstone to the Trump faithful. Speaking for “ nearly two hours ,” President Trump told his supporters that the Democrats were “radical left communists” whose party had been taken over by “crazed lunatics and radicals.”

Inspiring fear is an old tactic. Some years ago, Richard Nixon, a skilled practitioner in the art of political division, said : “People react to fear, not love. They don’t teach that in Sunday school, but it’s true.”

For nearly 40 years, Americans have reacted to the politics of fear. In 1992, 57 percent of voters described Bill Clinton’s election as making them either “concerned” or “scared.” Over half expressed the same emotions after George W. Bush’s victory in 2000; 24 percent felt the same after Barack Obama’s 2008 victory and 57 percent were just as disturbed after Trump’s 2016 win.

If Americans are afraid of each other, unity is impossible and accomplishments are few. George W. Bush promised to be a “uniter, not a divider.” Obama pledged that under his leadership that “we are, and always will be, the United States of America.” Joe Biden called upon his fellow citizens to “put away the harsh rhetoric, lower the temperature, see each other again, listen to each other again.” Despite their best intentions, each of these presidents failed to unite the country.

The politics of fear began with Clinton’s election as the first Baby Boomer president. He reignited the culture wars as abortion, gay rights, women’s rights and changing family lifestyles became points of contention.

Obama’s victory signified the rising of a new, multicultural America. But the joy of selecting the first African American president quickly faded. Fears became paramount as Republicans, led by Trump, claimed that Obama was born in Kenya and questioned whether he wasn’t secretly a Muslim.

Only once did Americans unify following the 9/11 terrorist attacks. But that unity became elusive as the U.S. began forever wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.

Trump has thrived on a politics of fear. In his case, it is fear of the other — the immigrant and the minority person — and the fear that the economic prosperity that once defined the American Dream is waking up to a nightmarish reality.

Faced with declining poll numbers , Trump has resurrected the tactic so effectively used by Republicans so long ago: fear of communism. During the Cold War, fears of Soviet and Chinese advancements gave Republicans seven victories in the 10 presidential elections held between 1952 and 1988 .

But Trump’s politics of fear no longer has the resonance it once did. Labeling Democrats as socialists or communists does nothing to curb the inflation Americans see at their gas pumps or read in their grocery store receipts.

Rather than being fearful, Americans are simply exhausted. Exhausted with seeing minorities beaten or killed on their television screens, exhausted with budgets tightening to a point where families must choose between food or gas and healthcare, exhausted with a government that benefits the rich and hurts everyone else and exhausted by the daily chaos of the Trump administration.

Voter fatigue is creating opportunities for Democrats to win in places where the party would least expect it. For example, in Florida’s 11th Congressional District, Democratic nominee James Pericola — a former student of mine at Catholic University — promises to protect Social Security and Medicare and bring a “common sense” approach to government. His opponent, Republican Joe Strada, is a wealthy businessman who promises to “ stand with Trump .” This 7-point Trump stronghold has turned what political analysts call a “solid Republican” district into a competitive race.

In an email to me, Pericola finds many voters exhausted by candidates “who duck tough questions and sell people out to enrich themselves and score political points.” Internal polling shared by the campaign shows a 1-point difference between the candidates.

Pericola is not alone. Other candidates who are running in districts long written off by Democrats are giving Republicans their first real test in decades. As the Democratic blue wave gains strength, it threatens to become a tsunami. That doesn’t often happen in politics, but when a tsunami washes ashore, it upends politics as we know it.

Following three decades of scaring each other to death, Americans are tired and longing for change. After a long run, the Trump Show may finally be over.

John Kenneth White is a professor emeritus at the Catholic University of America who writes on Substack . His latest book, coauthored with Matthew R. Kerbel, is titled “ Democracy on the Edge: The Trump Elections and the Future of American Politics. “

articles.title: Networks pull out of White House TV pool in solidarity with CNN
articles.summary: Major TV networks that rotate covering the president for wider media distribution say they will not do so moving forward after President Trump banned three media outlets from the White House last week. Fox News Media, ABC News, CBS News, NBC News and CNN responded to the ban in a rare joint statement, saying “the public…
articles.body:
Major TV networks that rotate covering the president for wider media distribution say they will not do so moving forward after President Trump banned three media outlets from the White House last week.

Fox News Media, ABC News, CBS News, NBC News and CNN responded to the ban in a rare joint statement, saying “the public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government.”

“No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting,” the outlets added.

The statement came after the White House pool said in a note to subscribers on Monday that “effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage of the President.”

“This follows the White House’s position preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties. There will be no replacement pool put in place,” the group noted.

The show of solidarity follows Trump’s decision to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House over what he says is “fake news” coverage of his administration.

Reporters for those outlets covering the White House over the weekend said their credentials were revoked , and they were not allowed access to the building.

Trump did not cite a specific story or segment that triggered the ban and said other outlets and reporters could soon be included.

The three outlets said early Monday they were preparing a lawsuit against the Trump administration over the ban, likely to be argued on First Amendment grounds.

The move has sparked widespread criticism from media watchdogs, free press advocates and elected Democrats.

Trump, in a Truth Social post early Monday morning, defended the move against the backlash .

“The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” he wrote online . “It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America.”

articles.body:
Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.), who is retiring from the Senate at the end of this term, will join the University of Southern California (USC) as a professor and co-director of their politics program, according to an announcement from the university.

Peters will co-lead the Center for the Political Future (CPF) alongside Republican strategist Mike Murphy. He’ll split his time between Los Angeles, where USC is located, and Washington, D.C., where the university has a campus near Dupont Circle.

Peters was a college politics professor before entering Congress in 2009. In a press release from the university, Peters said he is looking forward to helping USC expand its footprint in D.C. and educate students about the importance of bipartisan work and civil discourse.

“CPF has done a terrific job bringing people with different perspectives together,” Peters said. “I look forward to working with Mike Murphy to ensure we continue to have a forum where people can discuss tough issues, find common ground and actually accomplish something.”

CPF is focused on restoring civil discourse and practical reasoning to politics while preparing students for political life through internships, study groups, professional development and events. Peters will also teach classes on politics and policymaking.

The university pointed to Peters’s record of bipartisan legislative success, including 19 stand-alone bills signed into law last Congress. Murphy, in the announcement, said Peters is a politician who knows how to get things done.

“I very much look forward to working with him as we grow the center’s mission to teach and inspire USC students to embrace the idea that civility and reasoned compromise are far from the enemy of politics; they’re essential to turning political disagreement into practical results,” Murphy said.

articles.title: Outlets Trump banned from White House sue administration on First Amendment grounds
articles.summary: A trio of news outlets President Trump barred from covering the White House last week sued the administration on Monday, arguing it is violating the First Amendment and harming their ability to share information about the government with the public. In the lawsuit, filed in district court in Washington, D.C., attorneys for CNN, MS NOW…
articles.body:
A trio of news outlets President Trump barred from covering the White House last week sued the administration on Monday, arguing it is violating the First Amendment and harming their ability to share information about the government with the public.

In the lawsuit, filed in district court in Washington, D.C., attorneys for CNN, MS NOW and Politico argued the ban “could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles.”

The block “retaliates against protected newsgathering and speech in violation of the First Amendment,” the suit argues, noting Trump’s statements about the outlets he banned make “clear he implemented the ban to coerce more favorable coverage of the administration from CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO, and to deter other journalists and news organizations from reporting that the President might view as unfavorable.”

The president on Friday said the outlets were banned from the White House after publishing what he called “fake news” — a move that has been widely condemned by First Amendment advocates and other media organizations.

On Monday, the TV pool that covers the president’s daily movements said it was boycotting those responsibilities in a show of solidarity with CNN, one of its member outlets.

“The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government,” the networks wrote in a joint statement. “No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”

The president’s ban is “already severely impeding the ability of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO to cover the President and his administration,” the lawsuit argues asking the court to “immediately enjoin enforcement of the ban.”

The case has been assigned to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, the same judge who oversaw the White House’s temporary ban on a press credential belonging to former CNN reporter Jim Acosta during Trump’s first term.

Trump earlier Monday sought to justify the ban in a post on Truth Social .

“The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” he wrote, arguing the administration is instead “instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS.”

“It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control,” the president continued. “It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”

articles.title: ‘Got to be kidding me’: GOP officials pan Trump’s claims of shocking new election threats
articles.summary: Four days after President Donald Trump declared that his administration uncovered “shocking vulnerabilities in our election infrastructure,” dozens of state...
articles.body:
Four days after President Donald Trump declared that his administration uncovered "shocking vulnerabilities in our election infrastructure," dozens of state election officials from across the country gathered in Boston.

But they weren't there for an emergency summit to tackle the supposed crisis, even though the midterm elections are only 15 weeks away.

Instead, these election officials from 37 states met for a long-scheduled professional conference that struck a strikingly business-as-usual tone. In fact, Trump and his primetime address hardly came up.

In interviews with CNN, more than a dozen election officials from both parties said Trump's address surfaced little new in terms of evidence. Several GOP officials even scoffed at his presentation, pointing to the data that the administration released to try to bolster its case that there are massive numbers of non-citizens voting in US elections.

Matt Crane, a Republican who runs the Colorado County Clerks Association, said his text chat with a bipartisan group of colleagues was filled with "a lot of laughing emojis, and like, 'you got to be kidding me?' that this was all it was."

A GOP official from a state Trump won three times also panned the speech, which included the declassification of intelligence reports that Trump said posed an "unprecedented election security nightmare" with threats from China and Venezuela. (Trump didn't mention that the reports also made clear that neither country ever tampered with US election results.)

"I read the documents," the official told CNN on the condition that his state not be identified. "It was old. I've already seen this stuff. It wasn't new to me. We already had most of this information."

Democratic officials and election experts have condemned Trump for, in their view, escalating his longstanding attacks on the voting process, accusing him of laying groundwork to explain away any potential GOP losses this November.

Many Republicans who run elections have been far more circumspect in their public comments – broadly expressing support for Trump's stated goal of cleaning up voter rolls and preventing illegal voting, while defending their record in their states.

But in private, many decry what Trump is doing.

"We all know elections aren't rigged, but we have to keep our heads down and do our jobs," one Republican election official told CNN, on condition of anonymity, because they didn't want to anger the Trump administration.

The president's speech last Thursday, and a follow-up presentation from the Department of Homeland Security, singled out several states that supposedly had staggeringly high numbers of non-citizens on the voter rolls.

Trump has long peddled false and fantastical claims that thousands and perhaps even millions of undocumented immigrants are voting in US elections. Isolated cases do exist, but comprehensive studies from right-wing and left-leaning think tanks have concluded that this occurs on a tiny scale .

Still, the administration said it had reviewed public data and uncovered hundreds of thousands of non-citizens on the rolls in Pennsylvania and Nevada, and in California and New Jersey, which are Democratic strongholds. Some officials in those states have called for more transparency, demanding to know how DHS arrived at those numbers.

Even some red states that voluntarily turned over their voter lists to the Trump administration for examination were swept into the president's latest push. The administration said more than 28,000 non-citizens had been found on rolls in states with GOP election officials.

The DHS citizenship database being used to review voter rolls – called SAVE, or Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements – has a record of overstating the number of registered non-citizens. DHS itself acknowledges that states using the system voluntarily for voter-roll maintenance must further investigate any matches.

Sam Hayes, the GOP executive director of the North Carolina State Board of Elections who has aggressively backed several of Trump's election policies, said his team wouldn't rubber-stamp the administration's findings. He said the state, which DHS claimed had 1,599 non-citizens on its rolls, would conduct its own verification, which takes time and requires contacting registrants.

"There's nothing we accept at face value and just start removing folks" from the voter rolls, Hayes told CNN. "We've got to make our own independent assessment of this. … We still have to do the due diligence on our end."

Hayes also threw cold water on Trump's desire for quick answers, saying: "It's going to be tough to get it done by the midterms, but we're working toward that goal."

Georgia election officials told CNN the administration's claims about non-citizens on their rolls appear inflated. Of the 2,549 registrants flagged by DHS, they said, only about 20 had ever cast a ballot in the state.

Despite questioning the White House data, officials from both parties stressed that they take seriously their duty to keep non-citizens off the rolls.

New Jersey's governor announced Tuesday that a software error at the state Motor Vehicle Commission accidentally added about 6,600 non-citizens to the voter rolls, and that 400 cast improper ballots in recent elections.

The surprising revelation from a Democratic governor in a liberal stronghold immediately made waves and drew "told-you-so" recriminations from the Trump administration.

At a follow-up press conference Friday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin threatened fines and even potential "prison time" for election officials who don't comply with the Trump administration's demands for voter rolls and other election overhauls.

Election officials told CNN they take these threats seriously, especially after seeing the Trump-era Justice Department indict several of his political opponents. But at the same time, officials said, their focus is on their work.

"There is the concern about, 'Could I be made the example of?'" said Crane, the Republican who runs Colorado's bipartisan election clerks' association. "But I think, by and large, it's become somewhat white noise at this point."

A Democratic election administrator from a battleground state told CNN, on condition of anonymity, that he got a concerned call from his mother after she heard Mullin's comments about possibly prosecuting election officials.

Earlier this month, the Justice Department sent similar warning letters to all 50 states. Idaho's Republican attorney general was among those who pushed back, rebuking the DOJ in a sharply worded reply letter that said the "insinuations of criminal violations of the federal election laws are not well taken."

"Stop threatening your friends in Idaho," wrote James Craig, a top lawyer from the Idaho attorney general's office.

A GOP election official from another state told CNN that even some officials in red states don't feel safe, because of the Trump administration's unpredictability.

"It's extremely concerning when they talk like that, and we have no idea what they're going to do," the official said.

For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com

articles.title: Democrat Golden backs GOP’s Lawler in tough New York race
articles.summary: Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine) this week endorsed Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.), crossing the aisle to support the Republican in one of the closest — and most closely watched — contests of the midterm cycle. The move is sure to frustrate Democrats, who are fighting to flip control of the lower chamber and see Lawler’s seat…
articles.body:
Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine) this week endorsed Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.), crossing the aisle to support the Republican in one of the closest — and most closely watched — contests of the midterm cycle.

The move is sure to frustrate Democrats, who are fighting to flip control of the lower chamber and see Lawler’s seat as among the best pickup opportunities in November’s elections.

Writing Monday in a local New York paper, Golden said Lawler, who’s vying for a third term in New York’s Hudson Valley, is an independent thinker — one willing to shed partisan loyalties to get things done — and that voters should return him to Congress next year.

“He would rather pass a bill with the other party than score a point against it,” Golden wrote in The Journal News of Rockland County.

Lawler was quick to welcome the bipartisan support on Monday, characterizing Golden as a “servant leader.”

“Time and again when we needed bipartisan compromise, Jared was always there ready to deliver,” Lawler wrote on the social platform X. “I’m honored to have earned his support.”

On one hand, the endorsement comes as little surprise. Golden and Lawler are among just a small group of House lawmakers who represent districts won by the opposing party’s presidential candidate in 2024. And Golden, who is retiring at the end of this term, has long built a reputation as a lone-wolf policymaker, willing to buck his own party to advance legislation benefiting his purple district and bolster his bipartisan image.

Indeed, twice this month Golden joined Republicans on procedural votes to help GOP leaders advance their legislative agenda. In the first case, he did so to ensure that a proposal helping regional lobstermen made it to the floor. That bill was also championed by Lawler, and Golden leaned heavily on that dynamic in explaining his endorsement.

“There is not a single lobster boat in his district. He got no votes in this and no headlines back home,” Golden said of Lawler’s support. “He signed on because a historic American industry, thousands of fishing families, and the principle that federal rules should be built on facts were all on the line. And he understands that in every community, not just in Maine, mom-and-pop shops have been around for generations, and their livelihoods make up the very foundation of our communities.”

On the other hand, Golden is also a Marine Corps veteran who served in both Iraq and Afghanistan — a resume that’s similar to that of Lawler’s Democratic challenger, Cait Conley, a former Army officer who was deployed six times overseas, including stints in Iraq and Afghanistan.

In endorsing Lawler, Golden did not mention Conley. Instead, he bashed those lawmakers and candidates who place domestic threats above those from foreign adversaries. And he stayed focused on Lawler’s track record inside the Capitol.

Aside from the lobstering bill, Golden also singled out two other cases in which Lawler defied GOP leaders to endorse Democratic legislation: one bill overturning President Trump’s repeal of union rights for government employees, and another effort to restore the ObamaCare subsidies that expired at the end of 2025.

“Lobster traps, union rights and health insurance do not have much in common, except that on all three, Lawler chose to solve the problem rather than campaign on it,” Golden wrote in his endorsement.

Democratic leaders have a decidedly different opinion of Lawler and his legislative record. They’re pointing out that he’s sided with Trump the vast majority of the time, including in supporting the Iran war and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which slashed Medicaid and a host of other low-income programs.

Lawler was also among the rare battleground Republicans to appear at the Trump-heavy GOP convention in Dallas earlier in the month.

“Lawler has turned public service into his own personal payday and repeatedly put Donald Trump’s extreme agenda over New Yorkers, even when it means gutting his own constituents’ health care and driving up their costs,” Rep. Suzan DelBene (Wash.), the head of House Democrats’ campaign arm, charged earlier in the year.

articles.title: Climate, nuclear and pandemic policy can guide us through the AI threat
articles.summary: What is needed is a federal framework to check, oversee and control the existential threat AI might pose to society.
articles.body:
The buzz last week over artificial intelligence was the latest revelation that it could place the future of humanity at grave risk . The news invoked nightmarish scenes of AI taking over the world, using agents to carry out its own ends independent of human control like in “The Terminator” and other Hollywood epics.

If AI is potentially existential, then at least three other developments that threaten society loom as examples: climate change, massive pandemics and thermonuclear weapons. Consideration of each may offer insights on AI and how to control, if possible, its hostile potential and harness its value for humanity.

Climate change brought a great ice age. Whether a future ice age or global heating threatens mankind, it has in the past without AI.

Massive pandemics cannot be dismissed. It is not beyond the realm of possibility that AI could produce a fatal disease that is highly contagious and incurable. Frank Herbert’s “ The White Plague ,” written in 1982, posited a bioengineered disease that only killed women, suggesting something similar could be manufactured.

Perhaps the most relevant threat comparable to AI was the creation of thermonuclear weapons. It led atomic bomb creator Robert Oppenheimer to quote from Bhagavad Gita — a Hindu scripture featuring a prince at war who expresses “misgivings about the justice of killing so many people” — to show his pessimism about what lay ahead.

Thermonuclear weapons are indeed existential; they are potentially 1,000 times greater than nuclear weapons. But thermonuclear war has been avoided, partially because control was bifurcated over military and civilian use. President Harry Truman created the Atomic Energy Commission in 1947. It originally oversaw civilian usage but was replaced by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in 1975. Both the Departments of Defense and Energy oversaw the nuclear weapons complex.

Man-made pandemics and nuclear weapons require vast, complicated infrastructure that’s unlikely to be duplicated by individuals. And while severe climate change could be catastrophic, efforts to control greenhouse gases and other pollutants might have helped to deter some of the more dire consequences.

However, AI could make it easier to create man-made pandemics and could also impose huge damage to critical infrastructure such as power and water, which would threaten the food supply. AI in its current form could not likely build a nuclear weapon, but individuals using AI to tamper with nuclear weapons and reactors could prove disastrous. And hacks against AI infrastructure unprompted by humans are also frequent occurrences.

One solution, as with control of nuclear weapons, is to create an AI regulatory agency that puts out guidelines and is empowered with oversight of the industry. The degree of regulation will be a political decision. And, as with the International Atomic Energy Agency, this model could be replicated under the United Nations.

The Departments of Defense, Energy and Commerce, along with the CIA, would determine possible national security threats from AI and the appropriate responses to those threats. AI negotiations similar to arms reduction and control agreements could follow if properly managed. That would be far more difficult than nuclear agreements, as only a handful of states possess that capability. AI is more fungible and indeed could be exploited by individuals rather than nation-states.

What is needed is a federal framework to check, oversee and control the existential threat AI might pose to society. With the right foundations and leadership, just as a thermonuclear war has never been fought, perhaps a parallel outcome could be obtained for AI.

Harlan Ullman is chairman of a private company, and principal author of the doctrine of shock and awe. His next book, co-written with Field Marshal The Lord David Richards, former United Kingdom chief of defense and due out this Fall, is “Who Thinks Best Wins: How Decisive Strategic Thinking Will Prevent Global Chaos. “

articles.title: Vance defends Trump’s media ban as ‘totally appropriate’
articles.summary: Vice President Vance, who has long cast himself as a champion of free speech, defended President Trump’s ban on three outlets from the White House, calling the move “totally appropriate” on Monday. “He’s not banning media outlets. What he’s doing is saying ‘we’re not going to give you special access to the White House if…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance, who has long cast himself as a champion of free speech, defended President Trump’s ban on three outlets from the White House, calling the move “totally appropriate” on Monday.

“He’s not banning media outlets. What he’s doing is saying ‘we’re not going to give you special access to the White House if you engage in what is effectively propaganda,’” Vance told reporters at Joint Base Andrews en route to North Carolina.

“If you’re going to engage in what is effectively far-left propaganda, why would a Republican White House give you special access?” he added.

Vance’s comments come after CNN, MS NOW and Politico announced they were suing the Trump administration after being barred from the White House grounds last week.

“This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes,” the outlets said in a joint statement on Monday.

“Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting,” the statement continued. “Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.”

Trump defended his move in a post on Truth Social, writing that he was not instituting an assault on the free press but rather an assault on the “FAKE NEWS.”

When asked how Trump’s move is not an attack on free speech, Vance said the outlets “could still report on the Trump White House.”

“They can still get the public reports. They can still, of course, talk to people inside the administration and outside of the administration,” he said.

Vance went on to compare Politico’s coverage with that of the conservative outlet Breitbart during the Obama and Biden administrations, claiming Politico is as “anti-Trump as Breitbart was anti-Obama or anti-Biden.”

“Why on God’s green earth would Donald Trump be expected to give Politico special access when nobody in the media expected the Biden administration or the Obama administration to give Breitbart special access?” Vance continued.

“It’s about basic fairness. They can still report. They still have the access to free speech. They’re just not going to get an office in the White House anymore, and I think it’s totally appropriate, unless of course, they start to behave like real news organizations,” he said.

Breitbart has previously complained that it was not given regular turns in the White House press pool, which is determined by the White House Correspondents’ Association. But the outlet was not barred from the White House during the Obama or Biden administrations.

articles.body:
Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico has a slight lead over his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, according to a new poll.

In the NBC 5 Dallas/Telemundo Station Group poll , 46 percent of registered voter respondents backed Talarico, while 43 percent backed the Texas attorney general. Three percent backed a Libertarian candidate and 8 percent were unsure of their choice.

The Senate race in Texas has captured the nation’s attention as Democrats look to pick up a seat in a state that has been a challenge for them for years.

While Democrats usually have an uphill battle in the Lone Star State, Paxton comes with notable baggage. The Texas attorney general has been dogged by scandal, previously facing impeachment in the Texas state House on corruption charges before being acquitted in the state Senate.

The nonpartisan political handicapper Cook Political Report has rated the Texas race for the upper chamber as a “toss up.”

According to a Federal Election Commission filing published over the weekend, President Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., put an extra $5 million into the Texas Senate race. The money was earmarked for a Virginia political media company, Del Ray Media LLC, for TV and digital advertising targeting Talarico.

Paxton’s campaign has also received close to $54 million from the Republican-aligned Senate Leadership Fund’s Texas affiliate.

The NBC 5 Dallas/Telemundo Station Group poll took place Sept. 8-10 among 625 registered voters in Texas and had 4 percentage points as its margin of error.

articles.title: Trump’s Achilles heel is the stock market
articles.summary: While artificial intelligence leaders call for regulation to prevent existential risks, President Donald Trump continues to dismiss AI fears as a hoax to protect a stock market heavily reliant on AI speculation.
articles.body:
Over the last few weeks, something remarkable has been happening in the U.S. A burgeoning industry is coming forward asking for help in restricting advances in said industry. Think about how bonkers that is. Imagine railroad tycoons begging to be limited in their expansion. Think of Bill Gates and Steve Jobs asking President Bill Clinton to restrict advances to computing and the internet, or the tobacco industry telling the public before anyone else that they found out their product can kill you.

And here we are with AI. It isn’t just whistleblowers coming forward with shocking revelations and predictions about the end of the world. CEOs who are leading the charge into humanity’s greatest (and maybe last) technological advance are asking for help to rein in the technology that has made them rich beyond imagination.

The pushback from the American public had already been evident. The blowback against data centers is as non-partisan as a very partisan America can be. Students booed speakers at their commencements because they are fearful they won’t have jobs to graduate into. And plenty of Americans found themselves laid off because their companies’ claimed they were using, investing in, switching to or automating with AI.

The blowback was so bad that both Republicans and Democrats have spoken out on the campaign trail trying to position themselves as the least AI-friendly candidate. Except one.

President Trump has very forcefully proclaimed that the fears of AI destroying the world is a hoax . There does not need to be any type of moratorium, restrictions or guidelines for this new technology and he said the only thing needed was a “ High IQ” president .

Now, you can default (like many of Trump’s critics) to the “Trump is stupid” argument. How can he not see what everyone else is seeing? Why is he ignoring his own base who have howled against data centers in their rural communities? The answer has less to do with stupidity or cruelty and more to do with the fact that the “ AI bubble ” is something that has Trump spooked.

Look, right now we are dealing with high gas prices, high groceries and higher utility bills. But that’s not just it. Inflation is high, interest rates have gone up, and our debt has found a way to get even bigger. But the one economic indicator that has been positive has been the stock market.

Fueled by an AI boom, the market has survived tariffs, a war with Iran, inflation, and continued to grow. Even last week’s slide due to higher interest rates might be written off as a dip that will easily be corrected in a short time. The reason for this is AI. Plain and simple. While all these events in the world are negatively affecting Americans, AI has been pulling our economy up. Actually, it’s not AI itself. It is the speculation of what AI can do.

Although layoffs usually mean a drop in stock prices for companies, using AI as an excuse for layoffs means there are now mixed results for your stock price. Your stock might now go up, if you say the reason was an investment in AI.

The value of the stock market tied to AI is an astonishing 36 percent . And let’s be honest, a lot of that is speculation based on what people think AI can do, not what it has been shown to do. Predictions of a bubble have been around for a while, but with the bond market seeing yields rise, the party might be over.

And this would be terrible for Trump as the one economic laurel he could rest on would suddenly vanish. Remember when then-Attorney General Pam Bondi strangely yelled that the Dow was at 50,000 during a hearing about Jeffrey Epstein in February? That was a tell. The accusations of market manipulations with every Iranian ceasefire? Over 90 percent of the stock market is owned by the top 10 percent of Americans. And the top 10 companies account for 43 percent of market capitalization. And what are those companies banking on? Artificial intelligence.

A moratorium, implementation of safeguards, or restriction on AI can be catastrophic to the stock market and would affect the three groups of people Trump absolutely cannot alienate. The billionaires, CEOs and baby boomers with healthy stock portfolios would all suffer a significant amount should things turn south. He needs the billionaires and CEOs on his side. We all know just how much influence corporations have thanks to the Supreme Court’s Citizens United decision. And it seems inside the White House, they are worried about that leading to the announcement that there will be an AI Force to deal with the issue while not giving specifics.

No one should want the stock market to crash. It would hurt all of us and put us in a worse spot economically — and things currently stink. But for opponents of Trump, his actions regarding AI despite all the warnings and poll numbers revealed the Achilles heel that they have long been looking for. A slowdown of AI could potentially cause a correction, and Trump would lose the only economic indicator that he has been able to hang his hat on.

articles.title: Conservative ‘Squawk Box’ host presses Bessent on media ban: ‘We don’t do this’
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the White House’s ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from the White House grounds Monday on CNBC’s “Squawk Box.” Bessent joined the financial news show just days after President Trump banned members of three news agencies from the White House in response to what he deemed “fake news.”…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the White House’s ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from the White House grounds Monday on CNBC’s “Squawk Box.”

Bessent joined the financial news show just days after President Trump banned members of three news agencies from the White House in response to what he deemed “fake news.”

The media organizations said Monday they would sue the White House on grounds that the ban is unconstitutional under the First Amendment.

Bessent said he was traveling and wasn’t in the room when the decision was made, but that the American people have low trust in the legacy media because of its bias.

“The American people deserve good reporting, I couldn’t agree more.” Bessent said. “We’ll see where this goes.”

Bessent was pressed by anchor Joe Kernen, who said all presidents have had to answer tough questions from the press. He conceded that Republican presidents may have a tougher time with the mainstream media but that Democrats heed questions from right-wing networks like Fox News.

“I just don’t think this is something we do in this country,” Kernen said. “We don’t do this in this country.”

Courts that have considered bans on specific networks or reporters have often ruled in favor of the journalists. In Trump’s first term, the White House revoked the credentials of CNN’s Jim Acosta, who sued and was granted a court order restoring his access to the White House.

Bessent said Trump has been incredibly transparent while in office, with which Kernen agreed, and that the press “just don’t do their job well.” The secretary criticized the media for often asking questions unrelated to the White House’s talking points.

Kernen said just as Bessent was on the show to talk about policy and was now talking about the ban, the press will always question those in power whether their query is on topic or not.

“You can’t control the press,” Kernen said. “The press is going to press, the media is going to media.”

Bessent said the ban will be covered closely by the media, which he hopes will return to “fair and balanced” coverage.

articles.title: Both parties embrace Supreme Court spending limit ruling in midterm home stretch
articles.summary: Both parties are embracing the Supreme Court’s summer ruling that allows parties to coordinate and spend unlimited amounts of money with campaigns as marquee midterm races head into the home stretch. The Senate Republicans’ campaign arm is spending more than $45 million in coordinated expenditures with candidates, according to a campaign report filed Sunday. …
articles.body:
Both parties are embracing the Supreme Court’s summer ruling that allows parties to coordinate and spend unlimited amounts of money with campaigns as marquee midterm races head into the home stretch.

The Senate Republicans’ campaign arm is spending more than $45 million in coordinated expenditures with candidates, according to a campaign report filed Sunday.

The group is coordinating spending efforts with Republican Sens. Dan Sullivan (Alaska), Susan Collins (Maine), Jon Husted (Ohio) and Darline Graham (S.C.) as well as a suite of GOP Senate candidates, including Rep. Mike Collins (Ga.), Rep. Ashley Hinson (Iowa), former Rep. Mike Rogers in Michigan, Michael Whatley in North Carolina and former Sen. John E. Sununu in New Hampshire.

Meanwhile, the House Democrats’ campaign arm announced Monday that it would spend close to $8 million in coordinated expenditures in 26 battleground districts.

The group notes it has now coordinated spending on advertising for three weeks so far this general election cycle.

The Supreme Court ruled in June that political parties could coordinate fundraising and spending unlimited amounts of money with campaigns, saying that imposing federal limits was unconstitutional.

The ruling offered a massive win for Republicans who boast a fundraising edge across different party committees over their Democratic counterparts.

But the ruling was particularly beneficial for the GOP because the party typically fundraises through super PACS, which are required to pay a higher rate for TV advertising. The decision has encouraged GOP donors to give to party committees instead, where coordinated buys will be much cheaper than those initiated by independent expenditure groups.

Still, the ruling also helps Democrats as coordinated campaign fundraising and spending can ease some of their money woes via cheaper ad rates.

articles.body: President Donald Trump’s promise of a hefty payout for all Americans if Republicans win big in the midterm elections is taking heat from Democratic lawmakers who blast the vow as a "hysterical" lie and unlawful bribe. VOTERS HAVE A BLUNT MESSAGE FOR TRUMP ABOUT HIS IDEA TO DOLE OUT $5,000 CHECKS He continued, "The president will make any promises he can." Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., waved off Fox News Digital when asked about the checks, declining to comment. "$5,000 to gain a majority?" Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md., said. "He already has the Senate and the House and the White House, and it's been an unmitigated disaster." "It's just a campaign promise that he's trying to make to the American public, because he knows he's underwater, and he's not doing well and people are angry," Aguilar said. Most Democrats who spoke with Fox News Digital about the payments waved off the president’s $5,000 pledge as a "lie" and argued it's something Americans have heard from him before. "But lying to Americans around election season, what the president has done numerous times, I think it’s sad and shameful." ‘STILL WAITING ON THE DOGE CHECK’: BATTLEGROUND STATE VOTERS CAST DOUBT ON TRUMP’S NEW $5K PROMISE He continued, "I can guarantee you those checks ain't happening." House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said last week congressional approval would be necessary. "You've already seen House Republicans and Capitol Hill Republicans say that this isn't going to happen," Aguilar said. He also proposed excluding wealthy Americans from receiving the payout to make the pledge’s price tag more feasible. Democrats also scrutinized Trump’s prioritization, urging the president to shift his focus to deliverables for the American people — particularly emphasizing healthcare. "I'd rather give people their healthcare and their food assistance back," Subramanyam said. "That'd be way more than $5,000 for most people." articles.body: Critics, including parents of athletes, expressed outrage Friday after Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger's administration quietly shut down a rulemaking process that would have required school sports to be divided by sex. The move to end protections for scholastic sports based on sex is the latest development in the debate over whether biological males who identify as transgender should compete in girls' sports. "Governor Spanberger had a chance to stand up for women and girls, and instead she turned her back. VIRGINIA GOVERNOR ABIGAIL SPANBERGER QUIETLY ROLLS BACK YOUNGKIN'S PLANS TO PROTECT GIRLS' SPORTS Taylor focused on maternal and children’s issues during her time in Richmond and was the target of an assassination threat during her unsuccessful re-election bid last year. WHAT'S NEXT IN THE BATTLE TO 'SAVE WOMEN'S SPORTS' AFTER SCOTUS RULING — AND THE HIDDEN DAMAGE DRIVING IT "Women’s sports exist for women, and protecting a fair playing field shouldn’t be controversial," said Davis, R-Whiteland. articles.title: Lawsuit over White House media ban assigned to Trump nominee
articles.summary: The judge who will decide whether President Trump constitutionally banned a trio of media outlets from the White House is one of the president’s nominees — and he’s no stranger to Trump’s clashes with the press. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, whom Trump nominated to the federal bench in the nation’s capital during his first…
articles.body:
The judge who will decide whether President Trump constitutionally banned a trio of media outlets from the White House is one of the president’s nominees — and he’s no stranger to Trump’s clashes with the press.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, whom Trump nominated to the federal bench in the nation’s capital during his first term, was selected to oversee the outlets’ legal challenge, according to a docket update.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed the lawsuit after Trump said the outlets were banned from the White House on Friday. Their reporters indicated over the weekend they were being denied access. The suit claims it’s a violation of the First Amendment and their due process rights.

It’s a familiar landscape for Kelly, who oversaw the trial proceedings when then-CNN reporter Jim Acosta sued the White House in 2018 after the first Trump administration revoked his “hard pass” used to access the complex.

Three days after it was filed, Kelly ruled Acosta’s due process rights were likely violated. The judge issued an order mandating officials temporarily restore his credential. Later, the White House announced new rules for reporters and dropped its effort to strip Acosta’s pass. CNN then voluntarily dropped its challenge.

The case came just more than a year into the job for Kelly, whom Trump nominated to a federal judgeship in 2017 a few months after taking the White House for the first time.

The judge is a graduate of Duke University and Georgetown University and worked as a federal prosecutor before joining Senate Judiciary Committee Chair Chuck Grassley’s (R-Iowa) staff.

He also oversaw the seditious conspiracy trial of the Proud Boys, the far-right extremist group whose leaders stood trial over the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol. Kelly handed down a 22-year prison sentence for Enrique Tarrio, the group’s former national chair, which marked the longest of any Jan. 6 defendant at the time.

Trump granted pardons and clemency to them after retaking office. As Kelly dismissed the remaining Proud Boys cases this past summer, he wrote that “no one should mistake” his decision as agreement with Trump’s decisions.

“As the Court has said many times, the attack on the Capitol on January 6, 2021 was a perilous event,” Kelly wrote at the time.

News networks are standing in solidarity with CNN, MS NOW and Politico by not assigning a TV pool replacement for President Trump’s trip to New York City after he banned the three outlets from the White House.

The three major broadcast networks and Fox News are declining to assign a different White House pool camera crew to cover Trump. The news comes as CNN, MS NOW and Politico sued the Trump administration in response to the president’s ban.

The president has a busy week ahead, including a meeting with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) on the mayor’s home turf ahead of Trump’s attendance at the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday.

Trump will deliver remarks at U.N. headquarters Tuesday morning as a number of international issues — including the Iran war and Russia-Ukraine war — remain top of mind. The president will meet with leaders of Gulf states and, separately, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he’s in the Big Apple.

And this all just covers the first couple of days of his week. On Wednesday, Trump will begin hosting Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, about six months after his own visit to Beijing.

The two leaders are expected to discuss national security, trade and artificial intelligence during bilateral meetings.

AI is a particularly hot issue in the U.S. right now after researchers warned the technology’s rapid development constitutes a threat to humanity. The odds of a major breakthrough on AI security or safeguards during Xi’s visit are low, however, The Hill’s Laura Kelly reports .

Even so, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday the U.S. is proposing a notification system between Washington and Beijing on AI amid the concerns.

This is not the first time the president has threatened Iranian civilization.

What’s unclear: The agency has not publicly explained what prompted the officer to open fire, but it emphasized that Garces Perez was in the U.S. “illegally.” His attorneys argue that he was delivering food with DoorDash when the incident happened, local outlets reported .

The DHS is now leading the probe , with help from the FBI.

Austin wants answers: The shooting sparked protests across Texas’s capital, while local officials are pushing for more transparency.

Mayor Kirk Watson (D) pressed the Austin Police Department to help provide “clear, third-party eyes.” Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) is also calling for footage and records to be released — and warned against deporting Garces Perez, who is now in federal custody pending removal.

Billionaire stadium owner, Robert Kraft, did not like Macklemore, a Grammy-winning rapper, saying 'Free Palestine' on stage — so he made calls and the artist got pulled off of Ed Sheeran’s tour," the fundraising text obtained by Fox News Digital said. "This is not just about a single musical act. This is about how a small handful of powerful people, like stadium owners, can threaten someone’s livelihood in order to prevent an entire massive issue from being spoken about — in this case, the genocide in Gaza." COLIN KAEPERNICK ACCUSES NFL OF 'COLLUDING' AGAINST MACKLEMORE AMID 'FREE PALESTINE' CONTROVERSY She went on to say Macklemore's plight represents a wider battle between social classes. FORMULA ONE DRIVER LEWIS HAMILTON TELLS MACKLEMORE HE IS ‘STANDING’ IN SOLIDARITY WITH HIM ON PALESTINE "Oligarchs and billionaires could just as easily prevent people from speaking out about AI, workers’ rights, or any issue they don’t like. That is what makes this a dangerous precedent. This moment is a test of how far the very powerful can go in censoring speech," Ocasio-Cortez said. "And that’s why it’s important that we speak out about it. That we make clear that this is an abuse of power. And that we keep the focus on Robert Kraft and the way he’s using his influence to try to control what can and cannot be talked about in America." MACKLEMORE DONATES $1M TO PALESTINIAN AID ORGANIZATIONS AFTER ED SHEERAN TOUR FALLOUT The memo ended with the progressive congresswoman pledging to protect free speech and fight billionaires "who want to silence any form of dissent or peaceful protest," followed by the call, "Will you chip in $5 or any amount you can afford to power this movement for a better future?" Macklemore, who was made famous for his song "Thrift Shop" in 2012, said "Free Palestine" during a Sept. 4 show in New Jersey while opening for Sheeran's tour. He then performed a song inspired by the Columbia University anti-Israel protests, according to Forbes, then declared, "The people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them. I say: Free Palestine. I say: Free Lebanon. Free Cuba to the Congo to Sudan to Iran." ED SHEERAN SAYS HE TRIED TO ‘BUILD A BRIDGE’ OVER MACKLEMORE TOUR SPOT BEFORE VENUES SAID NO Kraft, who owns the New England Patriots and their home turf Gillette Stadium, then threatened to cancel Sheeran's show there, Macklemore later wrote publicly. Kraft also warned that other stadium owners would follow suit. And despite being told to stop, Macklemore said "Free Palestine" during the following night's show but clarified to Jews in the audience that his comments were aimed at Israel, not the religion as a whole. ED SHEERAN FACES GROWING BACKLASH AS RADIO STATION BANS SONGS, PROTEST GROUPS RESPOND TO MACKLEMORE'S REMOVAL It did not stop the backlash by pro-Israel groups and fellow musical artists, however, culminating in Macklemore being dropped from Sheeran's tour. Kraft later told NBC News that his boycott was about a broader pattern of public discourse that he saw as harmful to the Jewish people. He told the outlet, "I would welcome the opportunity to sit down with Macklemore and discuss the facts, because ultimately our goal is the same — peace for all people, an end to suffering, and an end to all hate." The pro-Israel billionaire also pledged $2 million toward helping Palestinians amid the fallout. Kraft also has close ties to Trump, despite a falling out over the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot. articles.title: Trump's Greenland fixation revealed as wars expose why the Arctic island matters now more than ever
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's Greenland interest spotlights critical minerals and oil as Strait of Hormuz disruptions threaten global energy supplies.
articles.body: President Donald Trump's persistent interest in Greenland has put a spotlight on what lies beneath the vast Arctic island, including potentially valuable deposits of critical minerals and oil. That focus intensified this week after Trump reached a security agreement with Denmark and Greenland that he is signing on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday — a deal the administration says is intended to strengthen U.S. influence in the Arctic and bolster long-term investment in the island. The focus on obtaining control and influence in Greenland, which also has a highly strategic location in the world, comes as wars in Ukraine and Iran expose vulnerabilities in global energy supplies and the U.S. looks to reduce its dependence on foreign sources of critical minerals. "One of the reasons that we are exploring for oil in Greenland is because of what's going on in the Strait of Hormuz right now," Robert Price, CEO of Greenland Energy Company and president of USFM Corporation, told Fox News Digital. Price's two companies are pursuing separate oil and mineral projects in Greenland, including plans to drill an exploratory oil well in 2027 and ongoing mineral exploration in the island's west. WHY TRUMP ZEROED IN ON GREENLAND, THE WORLD’S LARGEST ISLAND, MOSTLY COVERED IN ICE — IN 3 CHARTS Those projects are taking on new significance as conflicts abroad strain global energy supplies and highlight vulnerabilities in critical supply chains. The Iran conflict has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical artery for global oil supplies, while the war in Ukraine has put energy infrastructure at the center of the conflict. Trump announced an agreement with Denmark and Greenland on Friday that would expand the U.S. military presence on the island while keeping Greenland under Danish sovereignty. Full details have not yet been made public, but Fox News Digital obtained exclusive insights into some of the specifics of the agreement. "We don't want to be dependent on China for our rare earth minerals, and we don't want to be dependent on Russia for them either," Price said. "Critical minerals, they touch every part of our lives, which includes our cellphones, our computers, batteries, power storage, power generation," he said. Price's USFM has been drilling around Disko Island in western Greenland for nickel, copper, palladium and cobalt, commodities used in electronics, batteries, energy and manufacturing. "This mining district could be one of the largest mining districts in the world," he said, comparing its potential with Russia's mineral-rich Norilsk region. The scale Price described has not been proven, with exploratory drilling still underway. TRUMP'S AMBITIOUS ENERGY BET COULD BE A WINNING HAND AS THE WORLD BURNS MORE OIL, GAS THAN EVER Greenland's potential riches aren't limited to minerals. Price's Greenland Energy Company is pursuing permits for an exploratory oil well planned for 2027. Its licenses are on Greenland's eastern side, where Price said the geology resembles the petroleum-producing North Sea. "Our licenses are similar to the same petroleum system as the North Sea," Price said, noting that his company has sampled oil on and below the surface. But Greenland's value extends beyond what may lie beneath the surface. Sitting between North America and Europe and extending into the Arctic, the island has played a role in U.S. defense for decades. The U.S. maintains Pituffik Space Base there, its northernmost Defense Department installation. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Price said Trump's emerging deal with Denmark and Greenland could provide greater security and give companies more confidence to invest in projects that take years to develop. "What it does is it shores up long-term investment in Greenland, and that's what our projects are," Price said. "They're long-term investments from oil, gas, and minerals." "We're really excited about this agreement," he added.

articles.title: The Soros political machine is putting millions to work before Election Day — and zeroing in on key races
articles.summary: Tens of millions from the Soros family flow to Democratic allies as campaign finance records reveal over $40 million in disbursements before Election Day.
articles.body: Tens of millions of dollars in Soros-linked money are pouring into key Democratic campaigns and political groups as Election Day approaches, campaign finance records show. As of the end of June, Democracy PAC and Democracy PAC II — a pair of political committees created and funded by the Soros network — have disbursed over $40 million in donations to their Democratic allies, a review of campaign finance records show. Among the largest beneficiaries of the Soros-linked funding have been the Schumer-aligned Senate Majority PAC, House Majority PAC and the J Street Action Fund, the political arm of J Street, a vocal critic of Israeli government policies. Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who has made getting money out of politics a pillar of his Senate campaign, is also indirectly benefiting from Soros-linked money flowing into the Michigan Senate race through outside Democratic groups. MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL CALLS AIPAC DONATIONS 'LEGALIZED BRIBERY,' REMAINS SILENT ON OTHER DONATIONS Senate Majority PAC, which has received $9 million from the Soros-funded Democracy PAC this cycle, has pledged $30 million in spending to help elect El-Sayed in Michigan. "The fundamental corruption of our politics has been the system that allows corporations and would-be oligarchs and billionaires to buy politicians," El-Sayed said during a 2025 interview with a local news outlet. "I want to get money out of politics, put money in your pocket, pass Medicare for all," he told a reporter during a follow-up interview. El-Sayed’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Monday. The Senate hopeful is also scheduled to attend a Sept. 28 California fundraiser hosted by Jeffrey Soros – who is the nephew of billionaire George Soros. "Abdul El-Sayed is only for ‘money out of politics’ when it isn’t being spent on him. He’s wining and dining Soros billionaires and begging Chuck Schumer for money while Mike Rogers is taking on Big Pharma and calling for a suspension of the gas tax to lower costs for working families," Alyssa Brouillet, a spokeswoman for Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers, told Fox News Digital. "Mike Rogers is fighting for Michigan. Abdul El-Sayed is cozying up to billionaires and lying to Michiganders." The full scale of the Soros family’s 2026 political spending will become clearer as additional campaign-finance reports are filed. FBI RAIDS SOROS-BACKED VOTER GROUP’S HEADQUARTERS IN REPORTED FRAUD PROBE Another major beneficiary of the Soros family’s largesse has been the federal and non-federal arms of its Justice & Public Safety PAC, the primary vehicle behind its efforts to elect progressive prosecutors across the United States. ABDUL EL-SAYED DUBBED ‘VETERAN’ BY SOROS-LINKED PROPAGANDA NEWSPAPER DISTRIBUTED IN MICHIGAN The true extent of the Soros family’s 2026 political operation won’t be fully known until roughly a year after elections wrap up, as much of its spending is routed through 501(c)(4) nonprofits, a type of organization that can spend money on politics but is only required to release disclosures annually, often a year or more after the spending itself occurs. articles.title: Blue state gov ignites online firestorm with plan to send gov't into homes of newborn babies: 'Lunatic libs'
articles.summary: Massachusetts Democratic Gov. Maura Healey's Welcome Family program sparked a firestorm after a viral clip about home visits for new parents.
articles.body: Massachusetts Democratic Gov. Maura Healey set off an online firestorm over the weekend over a plan to expand the commonwealth's Welcome Family program, which she spoke about in a clip that went viral on social media. Healey made the controversial comments in an appearance last week on Boston Public Radio, where she discussed the state’s taxpayer-funded plan to send nurses into the homes of new parents after childbirth. "Everybody in the state, when you have a baby, you're going to have a home visit within days, weeks and that will be an opportunity for a healthcare provider to make an assessment to see if you need some additional support and resources," Healey explained. The clip quickly made waves on social media, with conservatives blasting the governor’s government expansion. GAVIN NEWSOM ACCUSED OF 'INFANTILIZING' PARENTS WITH DIAPER PROGRAM IN SCATHING WASHINGTON POST EDITORIAL "Does this sound like a good idea?" conservative radio host Howie Carr wrote on X in a post viewed almost 2 million times. "I’m sorry what?!" Conservative influencer account Libs of TikTok wrote on X in a post that was viewed over 2 million times. "MA Governor Maura Healey says everyone who has a baby will be visited in their home by a government appointed healthcare provider ‘to make an assessment’. Stay out of our homes you power hungry creep." "IDK who needs to hear this… but the government DOES NOT OWN your baby," Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C. posted on X. "Everyone needs to re-read 1984. " ‘COVID 2.0’: LAWMAKERS PUSH BACK ON SWEEPING HEALTH 'POLICE POWER' IN KEY BATTLEGROUND STATE "Lunatic libs," Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., posted on X. Fox News Digital reached out to Healey’s office for comment. Healey announced the expansion last week in a press release that described the program as "voluntary" and meant to "strengthen postpartum care and mental health support for mothers and families across Massachusetts, with a focus on reaching people earlier, making support easier to access and helping providers connect patients to care when they need it." Postpartum care has been a major topic of conversation in Massachusetts in light of the highly publicized trial of Lindsay Clancy in the commonwealth, where a jury recently deadlocked and could not come to a consensus whether Clancy was guilty of killing her three young children. Clancy's defense team argued that she suffered from severe postpartum mental illness. "Becoming a mother is a profound life change, and every parent deserves support—not just during pregnancy, but in the months that follow," Healey said in the release. "Postpartum depression, anxiety and other maternal mental health conditions are real medical conditions, and no mother should feel ashamed to ask for help or feel like she has to navigate this journey alone. We’re working to expand postpartum care, identify concerns earlier and connect families to the mental health support they need, because taking care of moms means taking care of the whole family." Amy Carnevale, chair of the Massachusetts Republican Party, told Fox News Digital in an interview that "this is an example of the government overreaching." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I'm a mom of three," Carnevale said. "I'm blessed to have three wonderful children. And, doctors, today, they ask about postpartum depression. They ask about the need for resources. So, there are plenty of resources available to women after they have children in Massachusetts and nationwide. And this example by Gov. Healey to send people into the homes of new moms is an example of government overreach and the Massachusetts Republican Party has been hearing from moms across the state, moms and dads across the state, really objecting to this new policy." Fox News Digital’s Amanda Macias contributed to this report

articles.title: Iowa GOP Senate candidate Ashley Hinson calls for Iran war to end despite voting to let Trump continue it
articles.summary: Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, has voted against House resolutions directing President Donald Trump to halt the war with Iran six times, including as recently as last week.
articles.body: Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, has voted against House resolutions directing President Donald Trump to halt the war with Iran six times, including as recently as last week. But on Monday, the Republican Senate candidate called for an “immediate end” to the conflict. “Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” Hinson wrote on X, calling for measures like suspending the gas tax, pausing diesel exports and replenishing the highway trust fund to provide relief from high costs. “These actions to lower costs are needed ASAP, and the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end,” she said. It drew a quick response from her Democratic opponent, Josh Turek, who also pointed to a seventh vote by Hinson against ending U.S. hostilities in Lebanon as part of the conflict in the Middle East. In a reply to Hinson, Turek wrote on X, “it’s easy to send a tweet but when you had the chance to vote to end this war, you chose not to.” “You voted seven times to continue it, including just last week. It’s time to actually end the forever wars and put Iowa and Iowans first,” Turek continued. “Glad you’re finally following my lead after waffling on the proposals I put forward last week to address the rising costs of the war in Iran.” Last month, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report with Amy Walter shifted its Iowa Senate race rating from “lean Republican” to “toss-up.” Trump won the state in the last three presidential elections, and Democrats haven’t won a Senate race there since 2008. Hinson’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment about her prior votes against the Iran war powers measures in the House. The latest resolution passed the House 220-204 last Tuesday, with seven Republicans joining all Democrats present in supporting it. Among those seven were Reps. Zach Nunn and Marianette Miller-Meeks of Iowa, who had previously opposed such measures but changed their position. Both are running for re-election in battleground House districts. The Cook Political Report rates their races as “toss-ups.” Hinson, a three-term congresswoman, has been increasingly characterizing herself as “bipartisan” and slowly distancing herself from the Trump administration as polls show voters disapprove of the president’s handling of the war and the economy. Her messaging and votes highlight the difficult balance of turning out Trump’s strongest supporters while appealing to the growing number of voters who have soured on him. Last month, Hinson objected to his proposal to import more foreign beef. Last week, when Vice President JD Vance went to Council Bluffs, Iowa, to rally for Republicans, Hinson did not attend, citing a scheduling conflict. “I want to make a shoutout to an amazing public servant,” Vance said in his remarks. “I know she couldn’t be here today, but are we going to elect Ashley Hinson the next United States senator from the great state of Iowa?”

articles.body: A smuggling vessel filled with Chinese nationals and other illegal immigrants was intercepted by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and the Coast Guard in what sources called a rare and "extremely dangerous" attempt to enter the U.S. through Florida. CBP confirmed the interdiction exclusively with Fox News, sharing video and photos of U.S. authorities intercepting the vessel, which was carrying 22 illegal immigrants, including 13 Chinese nationals. According to the agency, a CBP Air and Marine Operations multi-role enforcement aircraft first detected the vessel. The interdiction, carried out by CBP alongside Coast Guard personnel, resulted in the apprehension of one suspected smuggler, a Cuban national, 13 Chinese nationals, eight Ecuadorian nationals and one Dominican national. Sources emphasized to Fox News that it is extremely rare for Chinese nationals to attempt to enter the U.S. through maritime Caribbean routes that are typically used by Haitians, Dominicans and Cubans. During the Biden administration, Chinese nationals typically entered the U.S. through land routes in California and Texas, which are now subject to tighter enforcement under the Trump administration. CBP, COAST GUARD INTERCEPT MIGRANT VESSEL HEADING FOR PUERTO RICO; 40 APPREHENDED INCLUDING UZBEK NATIONAL Andres Blanco, executive director of Air and Marine Operations Southeast Region, told Fox News that "attempting to enter the United States illegally by sea is extremely dangerous and will not go undetected." He added that "those who attempt these dangerous voyages face arrest, prosecution, removal, and the very real possibility of losing their lives at sea." ICE-LED FLORIDA OPERATION NETS 500 — INCLUDING ILLEGAL ALIENS ACCUSED OF MURDER, CHILD ABUSE, CARTEL TIES After the operation, Coast Guard Lt. Corryn Ulrich, the commanding officer of the Pablo Valent, told Fox News that "the U.S. border remains secure due to highly capable teams and coordinated interagency enforcement" and that "we remain ready to save lives and enforce federal law at sea." The CBP Air and Marine Operations unit is designed to anticipate and confront aviation and maritime threats to America’s national integrity, according to the agency. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to meet Thursday in Washington, D.C. Gatestone Institute senior fellow Gordon Chang claimed that, despite the leaders trumpeting a positive relationship, Xi is mulling a war against the United States and organizing troops "for battle." "Xi Jinping keeps on talking about going to war against us… and also he's preparing China's society, civilian and military, for battle. And we think we're at peace," Chang said Sunday on "Fox News Live." "So, this is a very dangerous period for us." Chang’s remarks follow reports that China aided Iran in attacks that killed three U.S. troops in Jordan earlier this summer. The Department of Homeland Security said the man shot by the officer, Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, "illegally entered the country under the Biden administration and had a final order of removal during a law enforcement operation." articles.title: Trump’s approval rating hits record low amid Iran war, economy fallout
articles.summary: Republican support for Trump dips to 73 percent, down from 82 percent, as war and inflation concerns dominate polls.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 32 percent – the lowest of his ⁠political career – as his fellow Republicans soured on his handling of the cost of living amid the unpopular Iran war, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found.

The four-day poll, which closed on Sunday, showed 73 percent of Republicans ‌approved of Trump’s job performance, down from 82 percent in a Reuters/Ipsos poll a week earlier. His overall approval was 35 percent then.

Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 on promises to tame inflation and end foreign wars. In a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in the hours after he was first sworn ⁠in, he enjoyed a 47 percent approval rating.

Just ⁠17 percent of respondents in the new poll approved of his handling of the cost of living – the top issue. Americans say it will determine how they vote in ⁠the November 3 midterm elections, when Trump’s Republicans are defending narrow congressional majorities.

Dissatisfaction among Republicans has been growing since Trump launched ⁠the war on Iran in February, which has pushed gasoline and diesel prices sharply higher. Now for the first time, Republicans who disapprove of Trump’s handling of the ‌cost of living outnumber those who give him a thumbs up – 51 percent to 44 percent.

Trump said on Wednesday that the United States is “hopefully toward the end” of its war with Iran, raising the prospect of renewed diplomacy even as fighting continues in Yemen.

However, Tehran has not confirmed that direct negotiations with Washington have resumed.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted online and gathered 1,277 responses ‌from ‌US adults nationwide. It had a margin of error of three percentage points.
